speechtext:
['Mr. Speaker, the time available for the discussion of this bill, scarcely five minutes, will hardly permit any detailed analysis, and I do not purpose to attempt to do so at this time. Lest the time elapse before I have an opportunity of stating my view of the bill I shall reverse the ordinary procedure and, before giving my reasons, state that I am opposed to the principle of the bill and I shall vote against it. It is with some regret that I find myself holding the view that I cannot support a bill introduced by my good friend and colleague the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon), but there is a principle involved of very wide application.
The bill divides itself into two parts. One provision is that all civil service appointments, outside of appointments at Ottawa, shall be removed from the operation of the Civil Service Act. As to the remainder, that is to say, the appointments to the service at Ottawa, even in those cases the right of the commission to make such appointments is very considerably curtailed.
With regard to outside appointments, if this bill were enacted as introduced, what would be the practical effect? It would then devolve upon the member for each constituency, with such advisers as he may gather around him in the way of an executive, to recommend from time to time persons to fill vacancies. It would not be complimentary to other hon. members of this house to urge that, from whatever constituency they may come, they would not use good judgment in such matters or that they would not be competent to make good selections. The dangers from that point of view would seem largely theoretical. I believe that an hon. member faced with the duty of recommending a person for any position in his constituency would be guided by the merit of the individual who might be recommended. It may be urged that it is only natural that a member would nominate someone from his own political party. Perhaps that is quite true, but as I am quite prepared to concede that a Liberal member repre-

Unemployment-Mr. Reid
senting a constituency can find among bis followers men worthy of being nominated for positions of honour and trust, so I think they will concede that we on this side of the house can find such men among our own supporters.
Therefore it is not primarily the question of appointments in respect to which I am apprehensive, but it is the effect upon the service itself. If the political be the first consideration in the matter of appointments, when you come to a change of government the supporters of the member then representing the constituency in question, remembering that certain appointments were made first because of political considerations, will demand, and press that demand with considerable force, that, the new government having the right to exercise discretion and make a change, the change be made. In very large measure the principle will apply that "those who live by the sword shall die by the sword."']

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) I beg to move that you do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want at this stage to take up the question of unemployment in Canada and before I conclude I intend to move the following amendment:
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
That whereas the present Prime Minister of Canada in appealing for support in the election of 1930 made the following definite promises to the electors, in regard to unemployment:
At Victoria, B.C.-"You have my promise that if the Conservative party is returned to power that as soon after July 28 as possible parliament will be called together to deal with the problem of unemployment by providing, not

Unemployment-Mr. Heenan
doles, but work." "Is there any excuse for Canada to have hard times if the government is discharging its duties as it should."
At Calgary, Alta.-"I propose that parliament shall formulate a definite plan for permanent relief, and that parliament shall deal with this national problem and provide amelioration for the conditions in order that next winter the Canadian people may not be facing the crisis that is upon us without having a remedy at hand." "I am convinced this unemployment has now ceased to be local and provincial and has become national in its importance."
At Edmonton, Alta.-"I spoke of unemployment last night at Calgary," the Conservative chieftain declared. "We must face it absolutely at once." ... "I accept the challenge and I say again that I will call parliament together, at the earliest possible moment to provide at once the remedy-employment for all who can and will work."
At Moncton, N.B.-"The Conservative party is going to find work for all who are willing to work, or perish in the attempt. It is going to call parliament at the earliest possible date, after July 28 and take such steps as will end this tragic condition of unemployment and bring prosperity to the country as a whole."
At Moncton, N.B.-"I promise to end unemployment."
At Sarnia, Ontario: "Someone is responsible for unemployment; not individuals, but governments. Governments by their majorities in parliament are responsible for enacting all legislation."
At Quebec, Quebec: "There was no necessity for a conference on unemployment," he continued. "The solution was too apparent. What you want is work," he exclaimed, "not conferences, and you are going to get work.
"Unless his promises to the people of Canada were kept if elected to office," Mr. Bennett said, "he wanted Quebec and other members of his party to vote him out of office;"
That whereas notwithstanding the government demanded and received from parliament unlimited authority to use the resources of the treasury of Canada to such an extent as the government deemed expedient for the purpose of relief of unemployment, the measures taken by the government to eliminate unemployment have proven wholly inadequate and ineffective;
That the measures adopted by the government have involved an expenditure of public moneys out of all proportion to the employment provided;
That owing to lack of proper supervision and organization there has been partizan administration of the moneys provided by parliament for the benefit of those who were the most in need of work;
That notwithstanding the promise that these problems would be dealt with on a national basis, the government has shirked responsibility in that respect, by making a large part of the assistance provided to relieve unemployment, conditional upon contribution by provinces and municipalities, and has thus rendered abortive the relief which was solemnly promised to be granted on the basis of a national obligation;
That the giving of these solemn assurances, the using of them to secure support at elections and their violation after the attainment of office reveal a flagrant disregard of political 41761-28J
honour and tend to lower the standard of public life;
That the failure of the government to implement its pledges and promises has caused privation, want and suffering amongst thousands of Canadian citizens;
That in the opinion of this house the provision of employment for our people is the most pressing problem before the present government, and immediate measures effectively to relieve the serious unemployment situation should be presented to parliament by the government without further delay.
It will be observed, Mr. Speaker, that there are two features to my motion. The first part is a condemnation of the government for failing to fulfil its pledges to the electors. The second part calls upon the government to bring in immediately measures that will effectively deal with the situation. I want to offer my sympathy to the government at this time because any man or any party of men that undertakes to do a job with which they are not familiar and fails to accomplish it really needs sympathy. I know that my hon. friends on the other side are all recently converted to the idea of doing something for the workingman, but I once heard a prominent statesman, in fact, it was the present Prime Minister, say: Never trust a convert to do anything he is not used to doing, because he will always make a mess of it. On the other hand, there is sufficient of the milk of human kindness in my make up and I want to throw out a life line to save anyone who is sinking. To my mind the present government resembles a disabled ship at sea, tossed about on a wild ocean, drifting about aimlessly, but with the crew hoping that some chance wave will wash them safely ashore. If it were not for the fact that there are some few poor souls aboard that ship one might deem it a derelict. A derelict, as hon. members know, is a ship half sunk, without a soul on board; it is a menace to all other ships which are making progress. Unfortunately in the present case there are a few souls aboard this old ship, and I wish to throw out a life line to them. I wish them to heed the pleadings of their leader who said at Quebec during the election: If I do not carry out my promises to the electors, then I ask all the members from the province of Quebec and other members sitting behind me to vote me out of office.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
The trouble with the hon.
gentleman is that he had to walk the gang plank.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
The captain of the Conservative party, the present Prime Minister, is a gallant captain. He hesitates to leave the ship, and he stands on deck and says: Save yourselves, my boys; I will go down

Unemployment-Mr. Heenan
with the ship; it is quite evident, Mr. Speaker, that hon. gentlemen opposite will not reach out to grasp any life line that may be thrown to them. I am very much concerned with respect to some of my hon. friends opposite. I would like to save them if I could, and in proposing this motion I am giving them an opportunity to do the very thing which their own captain asked them to do when he pledged himself before the electors of Canada that if he failed to redeem his pledges he would ask his followers to vote him out of office. Here is one opportunity for my hon. friends opposite to carry out one of the government's pledges to the electors, by voting it out of office, for we all remember that the government said that it would end unemployment or perish in the attempt. There is no member, I am sure, supporting the government who will dare to stand up in his place and say, at least he cannot truthfully say, that unemployment in this country has been ended. On the contrary, the government's own reports indicate that unemployment is on the increase. There is no question in anyone's mind with respect to that because the government's very latest report states the fact plainly. Indeed, there is evidence of many other kinds to show that unemployment is on the increase, and those evidences are manifest to anyone who is observant. Railroad earnings used to be taken as a fair barometer of the condition of trade and employment within the country. Look at railroad earnings to-day, or at the number of cars loaded and the tons of freight moved, and you will find that the business of the railroads has decreased practically to the point where, so far as railroad men are concerned, they do not know but what they will be out of a job at the end of every trip. When the railroad companies were presenting their views to the Board of Conciliation and Investigation which inquired into the recent decrease in wages they stated in a public document that they had hoped for some improvement in economic conditions but that now they *were without hope, and in order to carry on they claimed that they must have a reduction in the wages of their employees. So the railroads, whose business used to be taken as a fair barometer of trade conditions generally throughout the country, have confessed publicly that their hopes for improvement have not materialized to any great extent, that they are hopeless of any improvement, and accordingly they have decreased the wages of railroad men in this country. I was at a meeting of railroad men not so veiy long ago, and I heard one gentle-

man say that at his particular terminal they used to have nine freight crews. To-day they have not one freight crew in the whole terminal, and the freight and way freight package business is being done by a mixed train. In my home town of Kenora there are engineers old in seniority who to-day are back working as firemen. To-day many old conductors are working as brakemen, and some men who have had many years seniority are entirely out of work, because they are not able to hold a position. Practically in every railway terminal in Canada shop men, maintenance of way men, car repairers and all sorts of railroad men are not being used. There is no question that conditions are becoming worse instead of better.
The relief measures adopted by this government have proved wholly inadequate. I recognize that in my part of the country men have been given work on the highways, and many are working for 30 cents an hour. As I pointed out time and again completion of the highway under construction was promised by the Ontario government to take place in 1926 or 1927. It would seem that at last some work is being done on that highway and I am glad. While I am speaking of inadequate measures, I should like to point out to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) that the residents in northern Ontario are being discriminated against. From the road work the people resident in those communities are receiving only two weeks' work out of each month while, on the other hand, those labourers sent into the district are working full time. I should like the minister to review that condition and see that the residents in those localities get a fair share of the work provided under employment relief measures.

speechtext: Does not my hon. friend admit that the expenditures made on the highway practically all remain in that community, the roads are all left there, and at least half or more of the work goes to the people in that part of the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend will have to get his wind up; I cannot hear him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Very well, I shall repeat my question. Will the hon. member not admit, first, that the product of the work is all left in northern Ontario, secondly, that the money is largely left there, and, thirdly, that a great part of the work is given to men in his locality?

Unemployment-Mr. Heenan

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I am not talking about that at all; I am talking about the residents in my hon. friend's district as well as those in mine and in every other part of northern Ontario who are not getting a square deal.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I will look after my own.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: They are not getting a square deal. They get only two weeks' work every month while on the other hand those men sent into the district are working full time. Only 30 cents an hour is being paid, and 40 cents should be paid.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Go out and tell the farmers that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Why not say 50 cents?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
If I said 50 cents my hon. friend would leave the chamber, because he never heard of anybody getting 50 cents an hour in his part of the country. The Ontario government has made a contract to provide food and provisions for the camps. Generally speaking, these contractors are bringing in their meats and other foods from the large centres, they are not purchasing hogs and beef from the settlers in that district, as was originally intended. When unemployment relief measures were brought forward by this government they promised that such measures would be directed towards helping people in communities requiring relief. In that promise, therefore, they have fallen short.
While I am speaking about wages I should like to point out to the government, and particularly to the Minister of Labour, that with respect to unemployment relief we have now a new principle announced in our fair wages policy. Throughout the world, so far as my knowledge goes and in every instance with which I am familiar, the fair wages measure has been considered as providing for a minimum wage. In fact, after attention was drawn to the matter by hon. members on this side of the house, the present government, in its regulations of 1930, establish a minimum or prevailing rate of wages. But what do we find in the new agreements? They provide for a maximum, not a minimum wage. For the information of hon. members I think it would be worth while to make a comparison of the two regulations. In 1930 the regulation was as follows:
All agreements made with provincial or municipal authorities involving the expenditure of any portion of the moneys appropriated by the act for public works or undertakings shall contain provisions for the payment of fair wages and hours of work in accordance with the intent
of the Fair Wages and Eight-Hour Day Act, 1930, and the fair wages policy of the government of Canada as set forth in order in council P.C. 1206 dated 7th June, 1922, and amendments thereto.
That is the prevailing rate of wages and the principle which has been announced and adopted by parliament on many occasions. At the present time however there is an agreement providing for a maximum rate of wages, and providing that the provinces and the municipalities cannot pay more than the federal, government is paying for work of a similar type. That represents a complete turn over. Whether or not it was done to fool the people, I do not know, but in order to have it on record I think I had better read it.
Fair and reasonable rates of wages shall be paid by the province and municipalities, but such rates shall not be in excess of the rates required to be paid by the federal government for the character or class of work in the district.
As I have said, this clause represents a complete turn over of principle as proclaimed in fair wages or minimum rates of wages regulations in any part of the world. Whether or not deception was intended, I do not know. There is one class of people however which is not deceived, and that is the working people of Canada. I should be pleased if the Minister of Labour would make an investigation so that proper adjustments may be made in rates of pay, and so that the working men of northern Ontario-because they are the men for whom I am speaking particularly-may receive rates of wages provided by this parliament and by the laws of Canada.
A few days ago I asked the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) a question as to the wages paid to labourers on federal public works in the constituency of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon). The minister very kindly sent me the information, and I find that in hi3 constituency labourers are paid 40 cents per hour on federal public works. I say to my hon. friend that so far as I am concerned I consider tihe workmen in my part of the country, in fact tihe workmen all through northern Ontario, just as good men and as much entitled to 40 cents per hour as the workmen in his constituency. Again I would ask him to see that the workmen of northern Ontario ibe given a square deal in that regard.
When we complain of these matters on the public platform or in the press, wthat do we find? We had the spectacle yesterday of the representatives in this house of the labour men of Canada being denied an opportunity

Unemployment-Mr. Heenan
to apeak. When the local member for Kenora and I complained of these things we aroused the ire of the Minister of Lands and Forests of Ontario to such a degree that at a board of trade banquet at Kenora he threatened the local authorities that he would spend the money appropriated for that district in another part of the country where it would be more appreciated if they did not officially repudiate what their elected representatives had said. Talk about intimidation! Could a Minister of Lands and Forests go into a constituency in any other part of th5 world and threaten the board of trade and the town council in that manner?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Can the hon. member quote anything to prove that statement, instead of just making it?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Yes, I will prove it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Well, go ahead and do so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I will prove it by no less an authority than the newspaper owned and edited by the defeated Conservative candidate at the last provincial election. It is all on the front page, but maybe the heading will be sufficient.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Read it all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
This is the heading:
There is lots of work to be done here, if we all work together. Will otherwise spend money where it is appreciated.
That will be found on the front page of the Miners' News of July 15, 1931.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: What does the writer say? Never mind the headlines.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: My hon. friend over there does not seem to grab hold of the life line yet.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Not from you.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I admire 'his spunk-stick to the ship until the last.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Your faith is not
very great.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
My faith in this government, to use a witticism, was dead long before it ever became a government. I have criticized working conditions in the road camps. True, those conditions have been improved since my criticism. I notice in the speech of the Minister of Lands and Forests to which I have just referred that he stated he intended to pay 50 cents a day in northern Ontario but because of some of us he had to pay a higher rate, so I am not ashamed of the position that I have taken in the matter.

I can prove every statement that I have previously made or make now with respect to working conditions in northern Ontario. However, I am glad to see that the great highway is in course of construction-the highway that we have been promised by our Conservative friends at every provincial and federal election since 1921. But instead of building one mile here, three miles there, half a mile somewhere else, just so many detached pieces of road, the work should have been proceeded with in a systematic manner. Goodness knows if any of these detached pieces of road will ever be connected together.
This government undertook to deal with unemployment as a national obligation. But in their very first bill they adopted a different principle entirely; they declared that unemployment is "primarily a provincial and municipal responsibility." In their last measure for unemployment and farm relief, the provinces and municipalities were required to share the larger portion of the burden.
I have not yet consulted the rules to see whether or not I am entitled to reply, but the motion speaks for itself.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: The hon. member is not entitled to reply. He is not limited now as to time; he can go on as long as he pleases.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
This	government has
reversed everything since it took office. Instead of giving work to the unemployed in the spring, summer and fall, they left them to sleep in the parks and to beg for a living or go hungry, and then they commenced their various relief undertakings in the winter time when the work could not be done in comfort by the men and with profit to the country. Then they have denied the workmen fair wages; they have instituted a maximum instead of a minimum rate of wages; they have given the residents in some parts, particularly those in northern Ontario, work on a half time basis, while newcomers are being given work on full time. Instead of dealing with the question of unemployment on a national basis, they have granted federal relief conditional on contributions being made by the provinces and the municipalities, and these contributions represent by far the greater portion of the burden. In short, while they pretend to give the provinces and the municipalities assistance with one hand, they are withholding it with the other; that is, they are withholding necessary public works that could have been undertaken at a fair rate of wages. They promised the electors that if they were returned to power they would treat old age pensions as a federal obligation. The cost of this to the treasury was estimated

Unemployment-Mr. Gordon
at one time to be 824,000,000 annually. Up to the present time the government have paid about $8,000,000 this year. Therefore they have been robbing the provinces of
816,000,000 annually. Here is another case where they are contributing with one hand and withholding with the other.
The government passed an act known as the Technical Education Act amid a great blowing of trumpets and beating of drums, but they failed to pay to the provinces the money authorized by this legislation. Is it any wonder that the ship is sinking? Now, when it is sinking, the government, not knowing where to turn and having failed to reach the port for which they set out, have turned to the civil service of this country, making them contribute in order to help them out of their dilemma. Last year they say they contributed $20,000,000 to the provinces, and in the estimates which have been presented this year there is a saving of about $43,000,000. The public service of Canada is suffering, and these civil servants who depend on their salaries for a living have to pay in order to make up the deficit caused by the mismanagement and bungling of this government.
So in moving this amendment I should like to point out that it is not only a condemnation of the government for its failure to live up to its promises; it is also a request for immediate measures adequately to provide for the employment of workmen in this country. We do not want the government to dilly-dally, as they have been doing, wait week after week and then at the last moment before prorogation bring down a bill asking for a blank cheque with nothing to prevent that money being sent out again and used in a partisan way.
In conclusion I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I hope every hon. member from Quebec on the opposite side of the house will heed the pleadings of their captain, take hold of the life line and vote the government out of office. Then they can go back to their constituents and say, "At least we carried out one promise to the electors of this country." Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), .the amendment I read at the beginning of my remarks.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot allow this occasion to pass without making some observations with respect to the address just given by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan). I do not forget the time immediately prior to the election of 1930, when I think almost every thoughtful man in
this country recognized the fact that things were not as prosperous as they had been in previous years, and while it is not my desire or my habit to go into the past in order either to build up a defence or make an attack upon my opponents, yet in the light of what has been said I think it would not be out of place to say a word or two with respect to the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite in the early part of 1930.
In the first place, the government became accustomed to the prosperity with which the world was visited during the years prior to 1930, and it was difficult if not impossible for them to realize then that a change had taken place and that this country was entering upon a period of decreasing business and lessened prosperity. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) then Prime Minister, in dealing with the subject would not go further than to say that there was an alleged condition of unemployment. But I remember quite well when the right hon. gentleman made his pilgrimage across western Canada. Each successive hundred miles seemed to impress him more and more with the seriousness of the condition before this government took office, until by the time he reached the Rocky mountains the right hon. gentleman was indeed convinced that we were in the midst of a depression.
What was the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite at that time? They did not recognize the condition, or were unwilling to admit it. As I remember the debates in this house, from reading them in the press and subsequently in Hansard, the substance of the remarks of hon. gentlemen opposite was that no one in Canada could expect a helping hand from the federal government unless their political views conformed to the views held by the administration of that day. That was the declaration made at that time.
There were a number of factors which contributed to the condition obtaining at that period. Some of those factors were entirely out of the control of any government or any individual, or of industry or agriculture. Some of them, on the other hand, were capable of being controlled and disciplined by governments, and I will ask hon. members to pardon me if I dwell once more on one subject with which I was very familiar at that time, I refer to the sulbject of immigration. I aim not unmindful of the fact that this country has two great railroad systems, with three transcontinental lines, two of them conceived about 1908. To-day I thank there is no thoughtful man Who will not admit that we are over-railroaded. So let us bear this in

Unemployment-Mr. Gordon
mind, that by reason of our projection of railroads across this country, whether we like it or not, we must get over to the positive side of immigration, because we must have more people if we hope to pay off the debt with wihich ten million people are loaded at present by reason of the railroad problem on our hands. That may not be a pleasant thought to those of us Who entertain a more modest and homely idea of our country, that is, that a nation is only a collection of happy, prosperous, Christian homes, and that its strength may be measured by the number of such homes within its boundaries. It is not a happy thought for those of us Who entertain that conception of our country, but whether we like it or not, if we are going to pay off that huge debt we must get over to the positive side of immigration as soon as we can. That opens up a serious problem as to where we are to get people who will be acceptable to this country and who will be easily assimilated into our national life.
What was the situation during the months just prior to this government coming into office? I think I am stating what was in the mind of every man who travelled within Canada when I say that the late government, not recognizing the condition that was becoming all too apparent, did not take any steps to curb the undisciplined flow of immigrants into Canada, which had been carried on for three or four years prior to 1930. I want hon. members of the house to remember this: During the sixteen months ended July 31, 1930, 221,561 people were brought into Canada, 99,367 of whom were adult males. This factor contributed largely to the unemployment problem which is facing this country today because if the figures are analysed it will be found that a large number of these people did not go into the open spaces of the country and engage in agriculture, where they could at least support themselves, but drifted into industry in the cities. There is abundant evidence of this fact in all the large cities in the country. It has been found that thousands and thousands of men and women have been here only a short time, many of them having entered the country immediately prior to the coming into power of this government. We are taking care of these people; they are not starving, no matter what anyone may say to the contrary. Immediately after this government came into power it took into consideration this one factor which was contributing to our difficulties. This problem was tackled in a determined and vigorous way. A vast system had grown up through the years to induce people to come to Canada;

connections had been made all over the world, particularly on the continent of Europe. The transportation companies were fully organized to bring people to this country and other associations were acting towards the same end. It was not an easy thing to curb this flow of people without creating some hardship and injustice, but this government did it, although in doing so it was subjected to a good deal of criticism.
The transportation companies did not like it at first, but since November, 1930-for the first time, as far as I have been able to determine from the officials of the department and from those who have engaged in bringing migrants to Canada-the transportation companies, both on the ocean and within Canada, have been working in harmony with the department in an effort to colonize at home and to clear up the mess which was left to this government by those who preceded us. The result has been that some 44,000 souls have been taken from the industrial centres and placed upon the land. This has not been accomplished by a state-aided system of colonization but by using the organizations of the two great railway systems and our own department. That large number of people are off the unemployment lists, largely through the efforts of the present government. I contend that that is not a mean contribution towards relieving the situation which confronts us, and it has been made without expense to the country.
The depression was easily capable of being identified in the spring of 1930, but as time went on it became something more than a local depression. While the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) may be twitted from time to time, as he has been in the past, for the speeches which he made during the elections, I say-of course hon. gentlemen may laugh and will probably sneer a.t my statement- that any normal depression would have been cured by the measures adopted by this government. However, no one could possibly have foreseen the world depression with which we are confronted. On top of that we were faced with the disaster which overtook parts of the western provinces, mainly in Saskatchewan. This government had to and was glad to go to the rescue of the people in western Canada. It was a great burden to bear, but that burden will be discharged by the government.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) has said that the government has done nothing to assist people to carry on through this period. Just as soon as it was possible to do so, this house was convened. A measure was passed permitting the govern-

ment to use the sum of $20,000,000 to take such steps, in conjunction with the municipalities and the provinces, as were deemed desirable and necessary to relieve unemployment and to assist the destitute and needy people of this country. That measure resulted in a total expenditure of $70,472,832-the federal government's share being $17,372,848 -on various useful works and the employment of the requisite number of men.
I feel convinced that if we can divorce ourselves from political partisanship, and I hope we can at a time like this-probably the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) can do this if he tries-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: When that does happen, it will be very much appreciated.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
As time went on it was
apparent that further measures would have to be adopted in order that those in want might be given such employment as would tide them over, and the result was the legislation of last session. Under that legislation, 334,301 persons have been given employment up to January 31, 1932, the total number of man-days being 7,415,973. The total commitments necessary to carry on the work to February 22, 1932, amounted to $76,426,387, the federal government's share being $32,822,847. This work is still proceeding. The figures I have given will be subject to some slight variation when the report is tabled, which I trust will be shortly.
Reference has been made by the hon. member for Kenora to the matter of the wage scale, and it has been suggested that this government has not adopted a course best calculated to preserve to the labouring man the standard of living and wage scale which had heretofore obtained. I would point out to the hon. member that he is losing sight of the fact that there is a vast difference between relief and wages. I am sure that this government will never adopt an attitude likely to destroy that which the labouring man has sought to build up through all the years, namely, a fair and honest wage and a decent standard of living. I think I can speak for labour just as competently as can the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, because I have been associated with labouring men all my life. In fact it was labouring men who sent me here and I expect they will send me here again. I know them; I am acquainted with their difficulties. For over a quarter of a century I have lived my business life right in the country of which the hon. member speaks, and I certainly do not propose to allow the statements made by the hon. member to pass unchallenged. I believe I was in that country actively engaged in various busi-
23, 1932
Unemployment-Mr. Gordon
ness avocations before the hon. member was, and I do not think I am boasting when I say that for many years I took an interest, as actively as my capacity would permit, in every public movement throughout northern Ontario, and not from a political standpoint. Anyone who lives in that part of the country knows that I had no thought of entering into politics.
In order that there may be no misunderstanding about the situation with respect to relief in northern Ontario, I should like first to refer to the speech of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of October 26, 1931. He is said to have made this statement:
"Never have I heard of nor seen such a gigantic political machine as the Conservatives have built up in northern Ontario," emphatically declared Hon. Peter Heenan, M.P., former minister of labour, addressing an enthusiastic political rally under the auspices of the Elm-dale Ward Liberal Association in the Knights of Columbus Hall, Spadina Avenue, Saturday evening. "Patronage has run rampant there and actually free speech is being prevented on political questions."
I do not think it is possible that the hon. member ever had his capacity for speech curtailed. He continued:
"Men and women are being discriminated against, intimidated and persecuted for their political beliefs; and that all under the British flag," Mr. Heenan averred.
The hon. member quoted from the Kenora Miner and Nation. Let me quote from the same journal in its issue of October 21, 1931, from an editorial referring to the criticisms of the hon. member with respect to the work in that locality. The journal from which the hon. member quoted and from a subsequent issue of which I am now quoting, makes this statement:
No more unfair or untrue statement has ever been issued by a public man than that given out by the Hon. Peter Heenan to the Fort William Times-Journal, October 13th. It could only be conceived by a mind filled by jealousy at the success of the measures taken by the provincial and Dominion governments to relieve unemployment in this district.

speechtext: These statements that were made by the 'hon. member on what I am told was his only visit to northern Ontario since the election-

Unemployment-Mr. Gordon

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
-of course came under the review of the responsible minister at Toronto who has this work in hand, and at the risk of tiring hon. members I should like to ask their indulgence while I read the minister's statement as reported in the Toronto Telegram of October 30, 1931. This statement was published widely and copied in the press, not only throughout Ontario but throughout other provinces. It is headed:
Northern Development Work at Kenora i Some statements recently appeared in the Canadian press from Hon. Peter Heenan claiming that the relief work being carried out by the Northern Development Department at Kenora is being conducted in a partisan way. Mr. Heenan is in the habit of making extravagant and reckless statements, and in this case he may have some excuse because he has only been in his constituency a few hours on one occasion in the last fifteen months. Anyone who is familiar with the situation knows that the statements are entirely false.
Last year Mr. Heenan and Mr. Hutchison, the Ontario member, made some similar charges, and, for the purpose of answering them and clearing up the situation, the Hon. Mr. Finlay-son, Minister in charge of the Department of Northern Development, went to Kenora at the beginning of this season's work and a public meeting was called in the town hall at which the mayor, the members of the board of trade, and a large gathering of citizens were present. Mr. Heenan did not attend the meeting but Mr. Hutchison did.
Mr. Finlayson fully explained the working of the system there and the local people were entirely satisfied. _ Mr. Hutchison sat through the meeting but did not make a single complaint or attempt to answer the minister. The citizens generally expressed their entire satisfaction.
The district of Kenora is the only district in northern Ontario where there is a member opposed to the Ontario government, and, notwithstanding that fact, last winter Kenora had more of Northern Development money spent in it than any other district, and the highest rate of wages in northern Ontario was paid in Kenora. This season, 1931, the rate of wages was made uniform throughout all northern Ontario, and Kenora is one of the districts in which the largest expenditure has been made.
On account of the large amount being spent on the construction of the trans-Canada highway in the Kenora district, we were able to take care of practically everyone in the district and also to send in a large number of men from southern Ontario for work on the trans-Canada road in that district. The department have felt that tins is a national work and the present situation calls for sympathetic treatment without regard to nationality, politics, or creed. In Mr. Heenan's constituency on the 24th of October, this department were employing 5,013 men on road work. As the total population of his constituency is given as 26,315, it will be seen that the employment is on a very generous scale. By far the greater number of these men are being paid half by the Dominion government. This is in marked contrast to the conditions that existed when Mr. Heenan was Minister of Labour and the Dominion government were not making any contribution of this kind. 
As to the selection of labour, this is done through the municipilities and is under the charge of the district engineers who are professional officers on the permanent civil service list and have had a great deal of experience and success in this work.
The department wish to assure the public that this work is not being conducted in a partisan way and is entirely above and beyond politics. Perhaps the best answer to Mr. Heenan is to quote three messages from responsible bodies in his own district who know far more about the circumstances than he does.
This is from the town council of the town of Kenora:
"The members of the Kenora council can truthfully say that as far as is humanly possible all detail in relief administration in the town is being carried out without regard to the applicants' nationality, creed or politics, and peace and harmony prevail among the workers, of whom fully ninety-five per cent are at work. We realize Engineer Lyons has a gigantic undertaking in the administrating of the work in our district, and are fully aware he is carrying it out as fair as is humanly possible, and we appreciate his efforts fully.
We regret that the Hon. Peter Heenan should have seen fit to give this untrue and unfavourable report to the press.
W. S. Carruthers,
^	Mayor."
. From the Canadian Legion at Kenora: "Be it resolved that the executive of the Kenora branch of the Canadian Legion of the B.E.S.L. deplore the statements made in the press that returned soldiers in the district are denied positions by the Ontario government rightfully belonging to them, and this executive are not aware of any such case and have received no complaints.
F. Gray, President."
From the Kenora Board of Trade: "Be it resolved that this council express its genuine appreciation of the much needed unemployment relief work being carried on by the government m the Kenora district and express our satisfaction on the non-partisan manner in which said work is being distributed by the association to those in need.
We also deplore any attempt at this time to create an impression that administration of unemployment relief in this district is otherwise.
J. Allan Sherrett,
Secretary-Treasurer."
I deemed it necessary in view of the very serious charges which the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River had made-because statements of that character, particularly when we are passing through a trying period, are only calculated to stir up anxiety, distrust and irritation amongst both those in affluence and those in obscurity, those who have plenty and those who are needy, creating in their minds, and very, very wrongfully so, the impression that those who are endeavouring to discharge the affairs of this country have their eyes solely on the next election-in view of these charges I deemed it my duty to cover other parts of Ontario.

speechtext: Are there no doctors over there to prescribe for those boys? If he had read all the correspondence it would have shown that those telegrams were in response to a telegram sent by the Minister of Lands and Forests.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Order. If the hon. member wishes to ask a question or correct an inaccuracy it is open to him to do so, but he is not in order in reopening the debate.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
I was not reopening the
debate, Mr. Speaker. I was simply asking the minister if he would not explain that those telegrams were sent in response to a telegram sent by the Minister of Lands and Forests.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
I deemed it my duty, Mr. Speaker, as one of the members for northern Ontario, to make inquiries from responsible people in other parts of northern Ontario, because I may say that the wholesale charge that was made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River gave me a great deal of anxiety. I confess that I was persuaded that he was probably carried away by the enthusiasm created by the ward Liberal association meeting which he was attending, but at the same time his charge was too serious to pass over. I therefore communicated with the centres where, if there was discrimination, if there was all this partisanship and persecution of the people, it would be most easily identified and known, namely in the mining centres. So I wrote to Timmins, to try to get a letter from the mayor of that town. I did not know who the mayor was, but I recognized him when the letter came back. His name is George Drew, a well known and very responsible man in that large town. I am told, although I am not sure of this, that he is a veTy strong Liberal-I hope he has changed his views. This is his letter from Timmins, dated November 14, 1931, addressed to A. F. Kenning:
Dear Sir,-
With reference to our conversation of a few days ago in regard to work being done by the department of northern development, I am very pleased to state that I have never heard any complaints or any reports of preference being given in the work due to party politics. I might also state that party politics has never
Unemployment-Mr. Gordon
received the slightest consideration in any rebel work which we are doing in Timmins, or when choosing the one hundred men who were taken from here by the northern development branch.
Yours truly,
George Drew,
Mayor.
I have another letter dated November 9, 1931, from Thomas McDonald. This man I know very well. He is president of one of the Liberal associations in the riding of North Cochrane, so I am sure that the hon. member for North Timiskaming will recognize the gentleman and probably be able to add some eulogy as to his party activities:
Dear Mr. Kenning,-
Re your conversation with me over the telephone regarding discrimination between Liberals and Conservatives being employed by Mr. Lough, district engineer, I absolutely cannot see any discrimination or favouritism shown to either party. Political affiliations have no bearing whatever in the securing of jobs in the electoral district of South Cochrane.
Yours truly,
Thomas McDonald,
Mayor.
I find another letter dated November 9, 1931, signed by the mayor and clerk of the town of Matheson. The mayor is the same gentleman who wrote the letter which I have just quoted. His letter is as follows:
With further reference to our telephone conversation of the 7th instant I have been unable to discover one single act of discrimination in regard to the employment of men in the northern development branch in Mr. B. Lough's district, and I am quite satisfied that it does not exist and that employment is given without any regard to anyone's political affiliations, but as far as possible on the particular capacity of the party applying.
Then I have a letter from the mayor of the township of Teck. Some of you may not appreciate the significance of the township, but it is in that township that the very large gold district of Kirkland Lake is located. Most of the larger gold mines are in the township of Teck. This letter is dated November 9, 1931, and reads as follows:
Dear Sir,-
Mr. J. W. McBain-
McBain is the municipal clerk in one of the largest gold-mining camps.
-has just spoken to me and asked if I had had any parties complaining to me that in giving work to the unemployed political discriminations were being made and that certain parties were being refused work by reason of their political affiliations. For your information I beg to say that no such complaint has ever been made to me by any person whatsoever.
Yours truly,
M. G. Hunt.
Unemployment-Mr. Gordon

Mr. Hunt is a very prominent Liberal in that mining camp and hopes to be a candidate some day, he says, although I still believe he will vote Conservative.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman
explain to the house how it is that there are so many Liberals in high authority in northern Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
I can answer my hon.
friend. There are many, many thousands of Liberals in northern Ontario, but they all vote Conservative.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: By the same token, I suppose all the Conservatives vote Liberal.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Going a little further south I caused a communication to be directed to the mayor of the town of New Liskeard. This town, as many of you know, is located in what is known as the clay belt, the farming belt of northern Ontario. While they are having a little difficulty in connection with the prices of products from their farms, yet I hazard the opinion that there is not a district in all of Canada-I do not say this in a boastful but in a thankful way-that presents a finer farming opportunity than that part of Timiskaming. Its fertile areas, thousands and thousands of them, fortunately have not passed out to speculators, but are still held largely by the crown, and are adjacent to such great markets as the mining camps afford. I thought I had written to the mayor of the town of New Liskeard, but I find that he wrote to me. His letter which is now before me is dated November 14, 1931, addressed to myself and is as follows:
I have noticed in the press certain statements said to have been made by Honourable Peter Heenan relative to political interference of men being employed on road construction in northern Ontario, and while I have no wish to enter into any political discussion, these alleged statements by Mr. Heenan are so untrue, in so [DOT] far as this particular section is concerned, that I felt I should write you stating the situation in so far as this municipality is concerned.
First of all, we were asked to register the names of the unemployed. Following this a representative of the northern development branch interviewed me, and in view of the fact that the municipality was to receive government assistance to carry out certain municipal work to provide employment, it was agreed that if the municipality would take care of their own married men the northern development branch would undertake to find employment for the single men.
This plan has been followed out, and is still being followed. As men apply for work at our municipal office, they are being employed in this manner: The unmarried men have been taken on without question by the northern development branch, the only requisite being [Mr. Gordon.}
that they present a paper signed by our town clerk certifying as to their place of residence. Certainly polities has not entered into this in the slightest manner.
I have further investigated sufficiently to positively say that so far as our residents are concerned there has been no political interference either before or after the employment of these men. Neither have I heard of any interference with men from other municipalities.
The arrangement has worked out very satisfactorily, and the government should be much complimented rather than criticized for their endeavours in this connection.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) H. W. Sutcliffe,
Mayor.
Then, I pursued the situation a little further and made inquiries from men whom I met as to the situation with regard to the work being carried out in that great country. As a result I can state to this house with a great deal of confidence that while there are some men out of employment, probably more than there would be in normal times, although owing to the seasonal nature of occupations in that country there are always some out of employment-the work in that part of the province is being properly administered, so far as it is humanly possible. The utmost efforts are being made to see that the work is given only to those who need it, and is carried out efficiently, and that the money goes the farthest.
While some people say that the town of Cobalt is on the down grade, I still think it has a long life before it. It is however a great centre for working men, especially miners, and a great deal of work is carried on in that town. On November 2, 1931, a letter was addressed to me by the mayor of the town of Cobalt. I do not know what his politics are, but I expect he voted for me. The letter is as follows:
Honourable Sir,-
I have read with surprise and much concern certain statements attributed to Honourable Peter Heenan in the Ottawa Citizen of October 26, 1931, and which embody sweeping denunciations of governmental administration of works in northern Ontario.
While I have no direct know-ledge of conditions in the western part of northern Ontario I can speak with a reasonable degree of confidence concerning the conditions as they are in this section since I have, owing to unemployment conditions, been in fairly close touch with road work and other development here. The w-ork is going forward apace and I have not found that political affiliations have been an impediment to the employment of any man or class of men otherwise qualified.
I feel further that the majority of people in this part of the province are satisfied with the conduct of affairs as at present administrated.
It is true and in the very nature of things that in the opening up of northern Ontario to travel and transportation and in the develop-

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
ment of our vast virgin resources the demands of local authorities on both governments are great and in all likelihood you will find these authorities rapping at the door of the government for some time to come but that is no indication of lacking appreciation for the sympathetic consideration of our appeals and demands in the past.
It is quite conceivable that a continuous harangue of unfair criticism may find willing ears in some directions but what I consider more unfortunate is that the wholesale charges voiced in the article above referred to may tend, if persisted in, to dampen the enthusiasm of those ministers of the government whose ambition has been to open up northern Ontario and lay open to development the potential resources of which we are so proud.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) R. L. O'Gorman,
Mayor.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
That is the reason for
the letter; there is a fear that the ministers of the crown may withdraw their assistance.

speechtext: The reason for the letter is my hon. friend's colleague over there.

speechtext: It is certainly unsolicited testimony.
