speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
I ask hon. members to
pardon me for having quoted at such length from these various letters and papers. Sometimes very little is contributed to debate by everlastingly referring to quotations, from here, there and everywhere. At times I have thought it would be more refreshing if an hon. member were to develop an idea of his own and let us have it. Whether or not we could agree with it, at least it would be original.
So far as the government is concerned, working in harmony among themselves and with the authorities both provincial and municipal, with the industries and transportation companies, with anybody who has confidence in the future of Canada-and he who has not, I am afraid, is not the type of citizen who will get anywhere in any country-this government will proceed to coordinate its efforts, with all its various influences, in one joint effort to see, first, that the needy and the worthy are taken care of, and that there is no destitution in this land; and, secondly, that through a persistent effort we will bring this country back to normalcy faster than any other country in the world.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I regret very much indeed that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) should have introduced this resolution in the form in which he has, because, as was almost inevitable, it has led to a discussion along party lines. From the cheers which I hear in the lobby outside it would seem that we are to understand that there has been a great victory by the Conservative party because the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) has answered uhe charges of the former incumbent of that office (Mr. Heenan). I am afraid however that in the midst of this partisan debate we are forgetting the original purpose of the resolution, namely, that something should be done at the present time for the unemployed in Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: That is not the purpose of the resolution; it is designed to make political capital.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Someone has just said that they are making political capital.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: No, I did not say that. I said the purpose of the resolution was not to help unemployment, but to make political capital.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I hear the statement of the member.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Was that a question?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
No, a
statement of fact.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman opposite will recall very distinctly that two years ago in this house my colleague from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) introduced a resolution with regard to unemployment that led to a debate of some six days, and placed the then government in a very embarrassing position. Indeed, I have sometimes thought that the Labour group must assume some responsibility for the defeat of the Liberal government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Don't fool yourself.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
We did call the
attention of the house and the country at that time to the failure of the Liberal government to tackle this great problem of unemployment. The Conservatives made a bid for votes by promising that they would cure unemployment. I will not say that they could possibly do so. I think the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) is quite right when he says that unemployment in Canada is part

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
of a great depression that is world wide in character; but I think in fairness he should have pointed out that that depression was already setting in when the Liberals were in power. It was already in existence when the Prime Minister, speaking across the country, promised that he would cure unemployment. At that time the Prime Minister did not recognize the world-wide character of the disease.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Did you?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
I don't know
whether we did or not, but I think a reference to the debates of recent years will show that we came a great deal nearer to recognizing the real position than did the majority of members at that time. All through these debates we have been stressing the economic character of our social difficulties, we are continuing to do so, and I am very glad to say that a large number of the members are beginning to recognize this aspect of the case. Certainly we did not then realize that the disease was going to spread as rapidly as it has, and I do not know that anybody else did. But we are pointing out to-day what I think is not yet recognized by the government-that this disease is not cured. In the speech from the throne the government is trying to persuade us that we are on the upgrade, that we need not expect to face any very serious difficulty in the future. We in this corner would like to point out that it is quite possible there may not be a return to the normalcy to which the Minister of Labour refers, and in any case it is not likely that any such return to prosperity will occur within the next few months. I do not know quite what the Minister of Labour meant when he referred to "normal depressions." It is most unfortunate if we have to concede that our present economic system postulates periods of prosperity succeeded by periods of depression. I am afraid that that has been more or less the case in the past, and it was for that reason that during the past few years we have endeavoured to point out the necessity of providing some form of unemployment insurance, so that when these depressions do come we would be able to safeguard the interests of the workers. Capital takes very great care to have its reserves, and I do not see why labour should not have its reserves also. Now, unfortunately, we have no time to prepare the machinery necessary to set up a scheme of unemployment insurance; we face a crisis which must be met within the next few months. As I understand the situation, the legislation which was adopted last session runs out in the course of a few days, and so [Mr- Woodsworth.]
far the government has given us no indication whatever as to what measure it proposes to bring down to meet the needs of the coming year.
One other point in the speech of the Minister of Labour that I should like to comment upon is that he distinguishes between relief and wages. I know perfectly well there is a theoretical distinction between the two. It is supposed that relief is something given by the community more or less in the form of charity, whereas wages are supposed to be that portion of production to which the employee is entitled. But I would point out to the minister that if relief wages, that is, wages paid on relief jobs, are lower than the normal rate, it is simply a question of time until the ordinary wages are dragged down more or less to the level of the relief wages. That has been very cleai-ly recognized by labour for a number of years, and under the predecessors of the Minister of Labour it was conceded that an attempt should be made to give wages on the scale then prevalent so that there should not be that danger. But apparently the minister has abandoned that plan and is content to allow wages to be paid on relief works that are much lower than those current in the various communities in which those works are being carried on. I say that such an arrangement is prejudicial to the interests of labour in this country, because if we have this pace set for the lowering of wages in one class of work, it will inevitably reflect itself in the other class.
The minister has said that the government has cooperated with the various provinces and municipalities. That is quite true, and I have nothing to say with regard to the charges which have been made as to the working conditions on relief works in northern Ontario. Possibly the scheme as a whole has been working fairly well. There have been abuses; some of those are not the fault of the federal government, but rather of the municipalities or the provincial government. But it is not that aspect that I wish to emphasize to-day. It is rather this, that something must be done in the near future, as the plan adopted last year has not been altogether satisfactory. For one thing, I do not think it is possible to carry on that plan for another year by reason of the financial state of the provinces. Several of the provinces are almost on the verge of bankruptcy. In my own province of Manitoba only a few days ago the provincial savings bank-which ought to be the most secure institution in the country-had to close its doors. I understand it has assets which ultimately will be realizable, and that the

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
accounts have been transferred to chartered banks. But it seems to me a most serious thing that our province is in such a bad condition financially that we have had to close our savings bank. How can we go on applying relief in Manitoba when the province is in that situation? In defending a certain policy the premier of another western province recently said to me, "I have to take this action whether I like it or not; I hate to be the first to declare bankruptcy." When the provinces are in such a shaky condition as that I do not quite see how we can go on with an arrangement which will call upon the provinces to contribute a very large proportion for relief purposes.
If the provinces are in a bad condition financially, the municipalities are in a worse condition. Many rural municipalities in the west are virtually bankrupt. Some of our cities-if the truth has to be told-have very considerable overdrafts at the bank, and they hardly know how to meet their expenses during the next few weeks, or how they can possibly balance their budgets. So I do not see how it will be possible for the municipalities to continue to carry the load they have carried in the past. Again, private agencies have up to the present given considerable assistance. People have been willing to contribute to charitable agencies; old clothing has been distributed; rentals have been paid; in some cases Christmas baskets and even steady food supplies have been furnished by private agencies. That is particularly true in eastern Canada, but the treasuries of these charitable agencies are becoming depleted, and more than that, owing to the general depression those who usually have given through those charitable institutions now are no longer able to contribute. So that is the situation we face, the private agencies not able to do so much, the municipalities, in the west at least, almost , on the verge of bankruptcy, and many of the provinces not knowing which way to turn and even having to come to the federal government to get help in order to carry on from day to day.
Now let me direct attention for a few moments to the actual situation which exists in my own city of Winnipeg, for example. The report of the unemployment committee for the city council for the week ending January 31, 1932, shows that on relief, as of February 1, there were 5,299 married men, an increase of 186 over the previous week; 5,145 single men, a decrease of 167 as compared with the previous week, and 598 women, married and single, an increase of 20. The relief spent
during the week amounted to $76,000. The relief to single men was not included in this amount, nor was the cost of looking after transients; that was the amount spent upon those having recognized claims upon the municipality. That is an enormous burden for a small city to carry, and that city cannot possibly continue to carry such a burden for much longer.
Notwithstanding the long drawn out depression an attempt has been made to treat the people resident in Winnipeg fairly well; at least I can say they have received a good deal better treatment than has been given in some other municipalities. But at the meeting of the city council on February 1 the rates were cut down; previously a small family received $3.49 a week for food, and that was cut to $3 a week. I believe that works out to 41 cents, or less than 5 cents a meal for each small family. I cannot see how any family can exist on 5 cents a meal, even though at present vegetables may be cheap and the farmer not getting a very high price for his products. In the parliamentary restaurant we have to pay 75 cents or $1 for a meal, and there are other restaurants in the city where each individual meal costs $1 or SI .50. This amount of 5 cents a meal is for a whole family, a man and his wife and perhaps a small child.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Someone across the way thinks this is a great joke. I can hardly see how any man who has a family of his own can laugh when I am discussing a matter of this kind, affecting the welfare of thousands of our fellow citizens. They may say I am a joke, if they like.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
We do not think it is a
joke; we did not hear it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
There was a laugh went up, and I do not propose to let derisive laughter pass unchallenged during the discussion of a matter of this kind.
Then there is another thing. In my own city a committee of women, in cooperation with the Department of Health, have been making some sort of survey, and it has been found that in some 1,500 homes a child is expected within the next few weeks. These homes have been able to provide nothing whatever for the care of the baby when it arrives, and the good women of Winnipeg are setting about making some effort to provide some infants' outfits in order that the babies may be wrapped in something when they are born. In a number of the homes they have nothing

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
for that purpose but newspapers, and some of the women have taken the ground that under these conditions the only thing is to attempt to have some method of birth control, because they say children should not be allowed to be born into the world where there is no provision made for them. When that position is taken by reputable women of the city of Winnipeg I say we in this house can hardly afford to laugh at the condition of some of these people who are faced with such a desperate situation.
In my own city recently they went further and adopted what I think is an altogether unjustifiable attitude. I am not blaming the federal government for this; I just want to set out the facts of the case. They asked each recipient of relief to sign the following agreement to repay:
In consideration of advances made or to be made to me, by or through the city of Winnipeg or any relief department thereof, by way of relief, I agree to pay to the said city on demand the amount of such advances, and I agree that a certificate by the treasurer of the said city shall be final and conclusive evidence against me as to the making of such advances and the amount and value thereof, and I hereby charge all my property and assets with the repayment of such advances of the value thereof.
That simply means that under the duress of starvation reputable men and women are being asked to sign a bond which places them in serfdom forever, because these people will not be in a position to repay even when they are working again. The normal wage of this country is not sufficient for that, so a great many never will be able to repay. The more conscientious will object to signing this document and will try in every possible way to avoid receiving relief. The waster, the man who does not care anything about his word, of course will sign, so it is really no guarantee that the city will receive payment, though it has a tremendously bad effect upon the recipient of relief. He feels that in his dire distress he is being forced by the city of his adoption to sign away his rights. If he has any little property that he has gathered together in the last few years it must be hypothecated to the city.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we treat the poor in an altogether different way from that in which we treat the well to do in this country, and this is the point to which I had reference in an earlier debate in this house, when I called to the attention of an hon. geptleman opposite the fact that when we were granting bonuses by way of tariff concessions to the great corporations, because of the depressed condition of the country or because of something in the industry that

the owners claimed would not allow it to compete with that of other nations, we did not insist that the amount given them should be later repaid. In this country we have given bonuses and tariff concessions to the tune of tens of millions of dollars. There is no doubt of that. We have given to large corporations during the past years, we have been giving enormous bonuses and concessions within the last few months, and we are not asking that ultimately they repay us; rather we take the general view that it is to the good of the community that they be allowed to carry on their business. But when it comes down to the workingmen of this country, who have no resources other than their labour power, we hold them up at the point of a gun, as it were, making them sign this document promising to repay. I do not think a document of that kind could be considered as legal; I do not think moneys given under these conditions would be recoverable. But that is what the working people of this country are faced with.
If all of us were poor, then I should not mind. A newspaper of my own city called attention to these things, while in another column they referred to the condition of the banks. For example, the dividend of the Bank of Montreal in 1891 was 10 per cent; it was increased ini 1919 to 12 per cent, and has remained at that rate while bonuses have been paid -from time to time. The Bank of Nova Scotia paid 8 per cent prior to 1900, when it was raised to 9 per cent; in 1916 the rate was raised to 16 per cenit and has remained at that rate. The Bank of Toronto rate was increased in 1911 to 11 per cent; in 1919 to 12 per cent, and has continued at that rate while bonuses have been declared from time to time. The Bank of Commerce rate was increased in 1906 from 7 per cent to 10 per cent, and at the present time the same rate prevails. The Royal Bank of Canada rate was increased in 1903 to 8 per cent; in 1919 it was increased to 12 peT cent, and has remained at that rate. The Imperial Bank of -Canada rate was increased in 1899 to 9 per cent; it was raised to 12 per cent in 1911, where it has remained while bonuses have been declared from time to time. I could continue to read these figures, but we are all more or less familiar with the -facts revealed in the annual statements of our banking institutions.
Many of our industrial concerns -have passed their dividends but some are still paying a very good rate, not being very far behind the peak of two or three years ago. As long as there exist in this country such lairge reserves

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
of wealth, I see no reason why the poorer people who are suffering from the depression should be given such miserable pittances or should be asked to mortgage their future.
During the war we were told that there had to be equal sacrifices, but many men took advantage of that period to grow rich. Majny purchased tax-free bonds and have been drawing very good revenues since that time; with the deflation of money which has occurred they are drawing to-day twice as much as they are legitimately entitled to. As long as there are these sources of wealth, the poor in our community should receive the first consideration.
In my own city a large number of people are receiving relief and this number is increased by farmers who have come in from all over the province to try to obtain relief. I have had them come to my own door in the last stages of destitution. These men have not been able to make a success in the country and have drifted into the city in the hope that with the larger population and more charitably inclined people they would have some chance.
What is true of Winnipeg is true largely of the other western municipalities. Just before coming to Ottawa I visited Regina, Saskatoon, Calgary and Edmonton, and everywhere it was the same story. Municipalities and the provinces are almost at their wit's end, and no prospect for the future.
I receive letters almost daily from the industrial towns of Ontario-I do not know whether or not other hon. members receive similar letters; perhaps as a Labour member I receive more than my fair share-and in all these industrial towns there are large numbers of unemployed who complain bitterly of the amount of relief they receive. I spent last week end in the city of Montreal and met some of those connected with the granting of relief to girls. This is almost a new phase of the matter to me, because while we have some women and girls unemployed in the west, there is nothing like the number which exists in some of the eastern cities. Large numbers of girls are .registered in Montreal-I had hoped to have the figures here but they have not come through-and a very small amount is being given in the form of relief. The social workers complain that these girls are practically being driven out into the streets and forced to adopt all sorts of questionable means to obtain a livelihood. That is a disgrace to a country as rich as we are told Canada is, a country which is rich when viewed in the light of the statements of our banks and financial corporations.
I had a letter only the other day from Halifax describing the unemployment situation there. I do not think it is as bad proportionately in the maritimes as it is in the west, but large numbers of sailors are unemployed in Halifax, some of them having been dismissed from our own Canadian National steamships. They are wondering what they are going to do next. These sailors have reinforced the number of the unemployed already in that municipality.
From time to time we have urged upon the government the necessity of a definite plan to meet this kind of thing. Unemployment insurance has been mentioned and the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has promised that this would be brought into force during the lifetime of his government. I should like to ask him whether or not any scheme is being prepared, or is he going to adopt the attitude that because of the hard times it will be impossible for him to implement his promise. I do not put forward unemployment insurance as a cure for unemployment; that has never been done by us; it is merely a palliative. However, I contend that the insurance schemes in existence in Great Britain and on the continent are a better way of handling the situation than is the scheme adopted in this country. This unemployment insurance has been referred to as the dole, but there is no dole so demoralizing as the dole given at the doors of our mission houses and soup kitchens where some of our people have to apply for help. The other has some semblance of dignity; a man who contributes when he is working feels that he has some right to the insurance. When your house burns down you feel you have a right to the insurance for which you have paid. The methods adopted here regarding relief to the unemployed are of the most haphazard nature that could be imagined, and I hope the government has not in view the carrying forward for another year of any such scheme.
I should like to deal for a moment with the demoralizing effects of charity without work. It may be that some of the higher-ups can accept a large salary for a nominal job- there are certain sinecures which exist even yet-without experiencing any demoralizing effect, but I am a bit doubtful. When a man spends day after day looking for work without success, when he is forced to hang around the unemployment agency, when he spends week after week and month after month visiting the soup kitchens, he is not only unemployed but usually becomes unemployable. But what about the wife at home? She is worrying over whether or not there will be a sufficient supply of food for her

450	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
family; she is faced with the necessity of having to go to some charitable institution to obtain supplies and having to submit to the inquisition of a charity visitor. Such visits may be very necessary from the standpoint of the municipality, but from the standpoint of the home, it is absolutely demoralizing. Yet this is the plan we are carrying out in this country.
The present arrangements will run out within a few days but no indication was contained in the speech from the throne or in any utterance of the Prime Minister as to what is being proposed for next year. The estimates indicate that there is an increase in the vote for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, a very sinister thing. It is quite possible that part of this increase may be accounted for by the fact that we are taking over the policing of Alberta. It is barely possible that some may be accounted for because of the proposal to take over the policing of other places. That I do not know, but it looks very bad to me that our police force, which is practically a military one, should be increased at this time. Surely the government is not taking the position that the way to settle this unemployment question is to shoot down those who are unemployed. Is that what this means? I see one or two of my hon. friends opposite shaking their heads. Probably they think this is not what it means, but what else are we to infer from these increased figures? If the force were increased and if at the same time there were any provision for increased constructive work, I might not be so apprehensive; but when we have no constructive measures and when, on the other hand, we have an indication of repressive measures, what am I to think? Last year when the military estimates were under discussion, I said that we had come to the point in this country where we had to recognize that the military were here, not for repelling some foreign enemy, but in order to shoot down our own people.

Hon. gentlemen

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE

That was said by

I have the rest

Those are the

The Minister of Justice

Yes, he made an

He said: We in Canada do not want to repel any foreign enemy; we do not have to have a military force; we have no enemies east or west; we have a friendly republic to the south, and so on. He said: We do not need any forces for defence purposes in Canada, we are not like some countries in Europe, and then he said this:
We maintain only such military, naval and air forces as are necessary for the maintenance of law and order within our own border.

Is the hon. gentleman
opposed to that view?

Unemployment-Mr. Reid

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE

That is not the

The hon. member speaks

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Yes, if the Prime
Minister permits me; but let me point out to some of his followers opposite that their leader was elected from the constituency of West Calgary and I was elected from the constituency of Winnipeg North Centre, and constitutionally, whatever may be the practice in the house, I have the same rights on the floor of this chamber as has the Prime Minister. Those who object to my speaking so often may well turn and ask how far their leader monopolizes the business of the house.
I want, however, to come back to this point which I think is worthy of consideration. I had, indeed, no intention whatever, until I was interrupted by hon. gentlemen opposite, of saying anything with regard to the tactics of the opposition, but when I am interrupted I am forced to resort to that. What I want to emphasize is this, that so far the government has given us no indication of any constructive measures.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Neither has the hon.
member.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: It is not according to British practice that the opposition should be called upon to formulate policies. We are given no opportunity of doing so. The government, I think they will admit, do not accept them when we do advance them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: You have none.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Yes, we have
policies. I have suggested one of them to-day as a palliative, that is, an unemployment insurance scheme instead of the present method of dealing with the question. My colleague the other day suggested another palliative, namely, a shorter work day. That was not accepted. We have suggested that instead of raising money the way we do, we should raise it by a steeply graded inheritance and income tax. That proposal is not acceptable to hon. gentlemen opposite, and so they tell us that we have no policies. I suggested that if we are to cut down the wages paid to the civil servants and to labour generally, 41761-291
there was no reason why the wages of capital should not be cut down. Supposing we cut down the wages of capital by 10 per cent; immediately there is an uproar from the other side of the house because they do not accept our solutions, our constructive suggestions. I should like to see-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I would direct the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that his time has expired.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this amendment in connection with unemployment, and I am sorry the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) is not in his place. I wish to refer particularly to the relief measures in British Columbia under the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act which was passed at the last session of parliament.
As hon. members will remember, the question of the seriousness of unemployment throughout the dominion was stressed at various times by many hon. members on this side, and in passing I might say with regard to this that rather an unfair statement was made to one of the municipalities in my constituency when, in answer to their request to Ottawa for financial aid and as to what steps were being taken to combat unemployment distress, they were informed on July 29 of last year:
Parliament has been sitting roughly five months and seldom has there been so much talk, so much obstruction of public business at a time when action was so badly needed. Happily the end of the session draws near.
These remarks were very unfair and uncalled for to be made in reply to the municipality of Burnaby when it was asking for further aid.
I wish to speak with particular reference, however, to the operations of the act affecting British Columbia and the serious condition of some of the municipalities which have been endeavouring to cope with an unemployment situation such as never was contemplated since their formation as municipal areas. When parliament met in 1931 unemployment was not a new issue. In the session of 1931 figures were given and many instances cited to show that unemployment had indeed grown much worse. I believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was seized of the acuteness of the distress and the general discontent prevailing throughout the dominion, and at his request parliament voted an unnamed sum of money in the form of a blank cheque, as the Prime Minister said it was not known just what sum would be required to meet the unemployment situation. He assured the house how-
Unemployment-Mr. Reid

ever that no one in Canada would be allowed to starve. The undue burden which had been placed on various municipalities up to the session of 1931 had been many times drawn to the attention of the government. It will be remembered that from the beginning of 1930 up to the session of 1931 both this government and its predecessor had maintained that it was primarily the duty of the municipalities to take care of their indigent poor. The situation in British Columbia by August of last year had assumed alarming proportions. Thousands of unemployed had congregated in coast cities like Vancouver and were living under conditions which were not at all good either for themselves or the cities. Immediate action was demanded by the cities and municipalities, which already had spent every dollar in an effort to relieve the situation. They had reached the end of their financial resources, and they besought both the dominion and provincial governments that further financial aid be given, or in the alternative they asked these governments to take over the burden of the unemployment situation. While no definite promise was made to any municipality as to what help would be forthcoming, I am of the opinion that the statements made by the right hon. the Prime Minister, which were given wide publicity in the press, with respect to the assistance which the various municipalities could expect and the proportions which the dominion and provincial governments would contribute, were relied upon. I have here a copy of the statement that was published throughout the province on September 5, purporting to give the exact words which the Prime Minister had telegraphed to Premier Tolmie of British Columbia. It reads:
Prime Minister Bennett wired Dr. Tolmie as follows:-
Then follow the exact words of the Prime Minister:
"As there appears to be some misunderstanding regarding the relative responsibility of the Dominion and provinces for relief measures, may I again point out that any effort on the part of the Dominion to undertake the direction of purely provincial or municipal undertakings would be in derogation of the constitutional rights of the provinces."
"We have indicated that we are prepared to make most generous contributions, subject to effective supervision, to enable the provinces to provide employment for large numbers of persons. We have further concluded that in addition to our responsibility for purely federal undertakings and assistance direct to provincial undertakings, we will contribute one-half the cost of approved relief undertakings, in British Columbia cities and towns, and will loan to your province the additional one-half, leaving to you the responsibility of making satisfactory

arrangements with such cities and towns as to their contributions, on the assumption that they will deliver to the province their bonds as security, and that treasury bills of the province will be delivered to our government for the one-half thus loaned."
"We are particularly interested in immediate action being taken to relieve the unemployment in large centres. Please advise what undertakings are now under way, and the number of men employed."
Some responsibility must be accepted by the Dominion government in this matter. * The government was well aware of the acuteness of the situation prevailing at that time and also of the financial condition of many of the municipalities. Knowing all this, and the government having received a blank cheque for any amount necessary for the purpose of relieving unemployment, it was felt that the promise of aid should have been carried out; but that it was not carried out is very evident in many districts of British Columbia. Later I shall cite a particular case in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, namely at Burnaby; and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that it is not the only municipality that finds itself in financial difficulties due to the great burden cast upon it in the matter of handling unemployment relief work. As to unemployment relief works carried out by the provincial government, I intend to leave that matter till another occasion. At this time I wish to speak with particular reference to conditions generally.
An agreement was signed on August 19 of last year by Hon. S. F. Tolmie, representing the province of British Columbia, and the Hon. Gideon Robertson, then Minister of Labour, representing the dominion, and was subsequently approved by order in council. It specified the proportion that would be paid by the dominion government on unemployment relief work and on relief work jointly undertaken as between the province and the dominion, and also the various amounts as between the municipalities and the dominion, showing in each instance the proportion which the Dominion government would contribute to all such undertakings. With that agreement I can find no particular fault, but I do say, Mr. Speaker, that the Dominion government should have accepted the statements and assurances given by reesponsible dominion cabinet ministers to some of the municipalities and to the province of British Columbia. The then Minister of Labour was the one member of the cabinet who was in closest touch with the situation, and it was generally recognized when discussing agreements with him that any recommendations that were acceptable to him would be approved by the cabinet. That certain promises of work and

Unemployment-Mr. Reid
schedules of work were given approval by the then Minister of Labour there can be no doubt. It would certainly appear that there was some grave misunderstanding in this matter which persists even now, notwithstanding the remarks of the present Minister of Labour.
I would like to draw the attention of the Minister of Labour to the fact that some of these agreements were approved, but not signed, in the presence of the Minister of Public Works for the province of British Columbia and the then Minister of Labour, the Hon. Senator Robertson. I will mention three or four of them in my own riding. There was the agreement with Richmond municipality which was approved by the then Minister of Labour and the province of British Columbia, involving an amount of $100,000. There was the city of New Westminster agreement, which was approved by the then Minister of Labour, involving an amount of $200,000. The Burnaby municipality project was approved by the then Minister of Labour in the presence of the Minister of Public Works at Victoria to the amount of some $400,000, although in all instances the schemes which had been proposed by these municipalities were almost 25 per cent and in some cases 50 per cent greater than the schedules agreed to by the then Minister of Labour. To show that I am not alone in my contention I should like to quote a letter sent out by the Union of British Columbia Municipalities to the right hon. Prime Minister, dated January 27, 1932. It reads:
Representatives of thirty-five British Columbia municipalities of the lower mainland and Vancouver island met provincial cabinet at an all-day session re unemployment. Provincial ministers allowed us to peruse all correspondence between Dominion and provincial governments from the time Senator Robertson, Minister of Labour, made certain arrangements and agreed to certain undertakings with provincial government.
I have read that first part and shall probably read the whole of the telegram sent to the Prime Minister to show that I and the municipalities in my riding are not alone in understanding that the agreements were signed or approved by the then Minister of Labour.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, some cities and municipalities had met the then Minister of Labour in company with the Minister of Public Works of British Columbia, Mr. Bruhn, and presented for their approval projects and estimates of relief works proposed to be undertaken by them. I say again that the Dominion government should have honoured these approvals, even if they were given in
only a verbal way; because if there was one minister capable of representing the Dominion government at that time, and especially capable of making agreements with any province or municipality, surely it must have been the then Minister of Labour, who, as I say, was more thoroughly acquainted with the acute condition prevailing from one end of Canada to the other than any other member of the cabinet.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce, another member of the cabinet, had been interviewed, and so far as I can learn he did not object to the schemes put forward. He also gave some assurance that so far as he was concerned he would do all within his power to have the projects sanctioned. He said he believed he had the support of his colleagues at Ottawa. The general impression was-and there were ample grounds for such an impression-that the work would be begun immediately as a relief measure for the thousands of unemployed in that province. It would appear that the provincial government had every assurance that public works on a scale never before seen in British Columbia would be proceeded with by the provincial government. About 170 camps were constructed throughout the various parts of the province. Tools, equipment, machinery and supplies were purchased in a lavish manner. As I have already indicated, however, that is another story of which undoubtedly more will be heard.
While there is no doubt that the schedule or program of work had been submitted by the various municipalities to the province of British Columbia and had been in its hands for some time, it did not reach Ottawa until October 2S. The Dominion government must have had some knowledge that relief works had commenced, and it was well known by them that there was acute need throughout the province. In fact, in some districts feeling was running so high among the unemployed that the urgency of the situation demanded some action by way of relief work.
A shock was received in British Columbia when the schedules for work submitted by the province, which included not only provincial projects but municipal projects as well, were not accepted. At least the federal government should have accepted those undertakings which had been accepted by the provincial legislature on behalf of the municipalities.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
May I call the hon. member's attention to the rule which prohibits the reading of speeches?
Unemployment-Mr. Reid

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am merely fallowing my notes. It may well have been that the program of works and relief measures which had been commenced by the provincial government, and for which large expenditures and commitments had been made, did not meet with the approval of the Dominion government. I am of opinion that perhaps there was some justification for that attitude; but I say that so far as schedules or relief works submitted on behalf of the municipalities were concerned, there should have been an acceptance in full. I say the full program of undertakings should have been accepted by the Dominion government or the Dominion authorities. The various municipalities in my opinion were in that regard unfairly treated, because in the first instance they were led to understand that if unable to carry out any relief projects the Dominion government would come to the rescue by giving them 50 per cent of the cost of all relief work, and 33$ per cent of direct relief expenditures. At the same time loans would be made to the provinces to enable municipalities to take care of the 25 per cent of the proportion which, under the agreement entered into, they would have to meet.
After submitting their program of works and in some instances going the length of enacting by-laws, the municipalities were in the majority of instances informed that the total sums as submitted and agreed upon could not be granted. This information was given to them after the Dominion government had stated clearly to British Columbia that the total amounts as submitted for all relief purposes were too great. The municipalities were informed that the amounts as agreed upon could not be proceeded with, and that their schedules of work would have to be amended.
Before I pass on to further subjects I should like to draw to the attention of the government the fact that many of these municipalities had gone the length of submitting by-laws to their people. One municipality I have in mind, that of Richmond, had been given an assurance of a total expenditure of $100,000, and had spent the sum of $54,000 before they were told that their total allotment would be only 50,000. The municipality of Coquitlam in the constituency of my hon. friend for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber) had submitted a by-law providing for the sum of $34,800. That municipality had purchased equipment and made all arrangements to begin work before they were informed that their program must not exceed an expenditure of $19,000. The municipality of Burnaby,
TMr Speaker.]
which in the first instance hoped to expend $780,000 under its unemployment work, and received permission from the then Minister of Labour to expend the sum of $400,000, were notified that their expenditures must be cut to $380,000. The city of New Westminster, which had submitted a program involving an expenditure of $400,000, of which the sum of $200,000 had been agreed to, were notified that their program would have to be cut down to $95,000. That city was hit particularly hard because it had made contracts for the buying of material, and had launched out on a program of work with the clear understanding, -and with at least some semblance of authority-that their claim for $200,000 would be granted. As I have said, after their program was under way and material had been contracted for, they were informed that their total expenditure must not exceed S95,000.
One cannot go too extensively into this subject because all the details of transactions, have not yet been placed upon the table. When New Westminster approached the provincial government asking why their expenditure had been cut they were told that Ottawa was responsible because a bridge was to be constructed in the locality of Ladner the erection of which would necessitate the engagement of about 1,500 men. As that project was to be proceeded with, therefore New Westminster would not require $200,000 for unemployment relief. Telegrams and communications concerning the erection of the bridge were shown to a delegation from the city council of New Westminster who visited the city of Victoria, asking why their grant had been cut.
I say therefore that the Dominion should have accepted the agreements entered into in good faith by the municipalities many of which had been given approval by the then Minister of Labour whilst in the city of Vancouver. The municipalities cannot be blamed for going ahead with the work. The distress of the people was of primary importance, and if the government had been taking any note of what was being done in that province they would have realized that when the schedules were rearranged a drastic cut had in some instances been made. Reductions to the extent of 50 per cent were common, while, on the other hand, other municipalities were permitted to proceed with the programs first submitted by them. Further, some cities and municipalities had their allotments actually increased. So that if the government's intention was to cut down British Columbia's allotment, that object was not fairly achieved on the schedules

Unemployment-Mr. Reid
as presented by the provincial government, because these schedules, as I have said, cut certain municipalities and cities in some instances more than 50 per cent, other municipalities were allowed to proceed with their original program as O.K.'d by the provincial authorities, and others again were actually given an increase over what they had originally asked for. In due time some explanation should be given by the Minister of Labour or by some other member of the government as to why British Columbia was limited in the manner I have shown. It was fully expected that between $7,000,000 and $8,000,000 would be spent for the relief of unemployment in the province, as it was contemplated that at least 20,000 men would be given employment, although over 50,000 men had registered. And they registered under oath. I have before me a copy of the oath if any hon. member would care to see it.
I now desire to confine my remarks to the misunderstanding that exists between the provincial and the federal government. It has affected unemployment relief work in the province and has caused considerable grief in some municipalities. When British Columbia b program of work was rejected it came as a bombshell and the premier of that province could hardly understand the decision reached by the federal authorities. His statement in the Daily Province of October 27, 1931, was that Mr. Jones, the provincial Minister of Finance, was then on his way to Ottawa. I might quote his own words when he was informed that Ottawa had not accepted the province's program of work. Mark you, this information came to him while Mr. Jones was on his way to Ottawa and had not yet reached the capital. Premier Tolmie said:
Mr. Jones has in his portfolio documents to prove definitely that the province did not embark on its present program and did not announce plans for extending the Pacific Great Eastern railway without full authority for doing so.
This government insists that the federal government, through Senator Robertson, Minister of Labour, and Hon. H. H. Stevens, Minister of Trade and Commerce, insisted on an early start on work and promised to pay half the cost. In one telegram the federal government said it would not accept any responsibility for further delay in public works.
The newspaper makes this comment:
It had been known here for some time, and announced in these columns, that the federal government regarded the British Columbia works program as too large though this was denied officially in Ottawa. What staggered the provincial government to-day was the report that, having summoned Mr. Jones to negotiate, the federal government had announced that it had rejected his plans before his arrival. This
was incomprehensible to the provincial authorities and made them wonder what would come out of Mr. Jones' mission.
Regarding that misunderstanding, I am going to cite one clear cut example-its effect on the municipality of Burnaby. The municipality were given to understand that before they started work they would be financed either by the province or by the dominion. They were told on good authority to formulate their plans and that a loan would be made them up to any amount which they cared to take. With this understanding they approved a program of $400,000. I have not time to place on Hansard the number of telegrams that passed between the municipality, the provincial government, and the Dominion government, but the size of the file I hold in my hand will give hon. members some idea of the number of messages sent. So bad did the situation become that the bank told the municipality they would not accept the word of the provincial government in regard to finances. On receiving this intimation the municipality shut down the work. The municipality financed the whole project, although given to understand that if they contributed 25 per cent the provincial government would give bonds to the Dominion government for their proportion. The municipality have spent a total of $311,000 on that program, towards which they have received only $132,125 up to the 21st of this month. They are spending a thousand dollars a day on direct relief, and have been called upon to bear the whole of that capital expenditure. Their council have been almost distracted in their endeavour to cope with this embarrassing situation. That some misunderstanding does prevail is evident from a telegram sent to the reeve of the municipality by the Hon.
S.	F. Tolmie on January 21, showing that not only he but his Minister of Finance were under the impression that the money sent by the federal government had been intended for some other purpose, and not to pay any share of the municipality's proportion of the relief work undertaken. The premier told the municipal authorities that as soon as he received a cheque from the federal government the municipality would be paid. He has told them that all the vouchers have been sent to Ottawa and that the provincial government has borne any expenditure which has been made by the municipality. In spite of the statements made by the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) a few days ago to the effect that over $2,500,000 dollars has been spent, the provincial government still assert that they are awaiting payment from the
Unemployment-Mr. Reid

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, February 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gagnon for the second reading of Bill No. 14, to amend the Civil Service Act.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT
subsubtopic: EXCLUSION OF OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few evenings ago when the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) moved the second reading of this bill, I expressed some astonishment that such a proposal should come from a member of the Conservative party, the party chiefly responsible for the placing upon the statute book of the Civil Service Act. It is to the credit of that party that it has always shown unswerving allegiance to the merit system. I am tempted to ask the question: What is the attitude of the government to-day towards this particular measure? It is well known that last year the attitude was adverse, but I am not so sure what it is this year; although it is almost unthinkable that that party should reverse its well known policy.
During his remarks the hon. member for Dorchester stated that certain doubts which had existed as to the attitude of the government towards this bill had been removed. What was the doubt as to the attitude of the government which has been removed? Was it that the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) intended to have this bill go to the committee with the appearance of having passed the second reading, when in fact it had not passed? I do not know what was meant, but

Civil Service Act-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
there is a sinister sound in the suggestion tha:t the attitude of the government has changed. I sincerely hope that it has not changed.
I was disappointed in hearing the hon. member draw Doctor Grant into the discussion as being a supporter of a measure of this kind. Doctor Grant of Upper Canada college has been a supporter of the merit principle all his life. He has fought for it unswervingly for many years and the attempt to use any writings or sayings of his in support of a bill of this kind is nothing but a misrepresentation of his position. I have since secured copies of the articles from which the hon. member quoted, which quotations I challenged at the time. If any hon. member will read Doctor Grant's statements he will find that there is not one single line or sentence which challenges the merit principle of the Civil Service Act. All that Doctor Grant does is to challenge the administration of the act under the present commission.
I share many of the views held by Doctor Grant in that connection. I would point out that this bill does not in any way alter the position of the commission. The hon. member does not suggest what Doctor Grant has suggested, a one-man commission; he asks that the commission continue with abbreviated powers, that it shall administer to a certain degree the inside service but that the work in connection with the outside service and in connection with the merit system generally be put aside.
The hon. member alleged that this bill embodied the recommendations made by the Senate committee of 1924, known as the Beique committee, and by the Malcolm committee of 1923. When the hon. member made that statement I realized that he had not read the reports of these committees, much less the evidence upon which they were based. The only possible similarity between either of these reports and the bill is the second paragraph of the bill, which repeats almost word for word one section of the recommendations of the Senate committee of 1924. I could find no similarity in the Malcolm report. The Senate committee's recommendations were made in an effort to cut down the number of civil servants and not to jeopardize the principle of the Civil Sendee Act.
In discussing the general administration of the act the hon. member gave one or two pithy illustrations which seemed to amuse the house at the time. Hon. members who were present will remember his reference to the recent vacancy of the position of chief page of this house. To the intense amusement of those hon. members around him, and I regret to say of some to my right, he told a story of how candidates were asked to write an essay on the League of Nations, which story was received with loud ridicule. I have made it my business to secure a copy of the examination paper, and I have it before me. It is a perfectly understandable and comprehensive examination for a position of this kind. The hon. member did not explain that the position of chief page in this house is one of some little responsibility, as it concerns the comfort and convenience of the members of this chamber. The chief page must be able to direct the minor pages where to secure the necessary material which may be required by hon. members, and he must have some knowledge of what hon. members are talking about. In order that it might be assured that an efficient person should be in charge of the pages of this house, the commission submitted the following examination paper, upon which I challenge any hon. member to cast ridicule. The first question is:
Tell what you know of any three of the following:
It is significant that the hon. member was not quite accurate in his statement; he said the candidates had to write an essay on the League of Nations, whereas they could select any three of the following subjects upon which to write:
The recent activities of the League of Nations; the present British government; Remembrance Day; shipping wheat via the Hudson bay route.
That is perhaps the only ridiculous item. The question continues:
The National Service Loan; the 1931 census.
The second question is a collection of names and numbers which are to be arranged in alphabetical and numerical sequence. Questions 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 are problems in simple arithmetic; surely this qualification should be required of the chief page. Question No. 8 is as follows:
(a)	How- many members are there in the House of Commons?
(b)	How is the number of members for each province determined?
My French Canadian colleagues would certainly agree a question like that might well be asked of any page of the house, much less a chief of pages. Then there are these questions:
9.	(a) What is the seating arrangement of the House of Commons?
(b) On which side of the speaker's chair do the government members sit?
10.	Who is the speaker in the present House of Commons? the government leader? the leader of the opposition?
458	COMMONS
Civil Service Act-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
Surely these are intelligible questions to ask.
11.	Give the names of five cabinet ministers and the departments they administer.
An examination of this kind might well be one of the qualifications for a member of 'the House of Commons, and especially for some civil servants; because I had in my office one who claimed he had been sixteen years in the civil service and he did not know the name of the Minister of Immigration in the last government.
12.	Explain briefly any five of the following with reference to parliamentary procedure: mace; quorum; division; adjournment; prorogation: dissolution; legal limitation of duration of parliament.
Therefore I submit the hon. member for Dorchester has completely failed to make any case on the basis of his facetious remarks about the League of Nations and the chief of pages of the house.
The next reference he made was one that could have been made only by a man who did not acquaint himself with the facts but who relied on hearsay evidence or statements of some persons who had filled him up with stories of this kind. I am quoting from his speech in connection with a vacancy for the position of expert mechanic in the marine signals branch in the Department of Marine at Quebec. He said:
One of the three men who were appointed to act as examiners was the janitor of St. Patrick's church in the city of Quebec.
Surely the hon. member could have verified that before he made the statement. A person who was not a friend of the Civil Service Act must have prompted the suggestion, and my hon. friend used it. As a matter of fact the following is what took place, because I inquired of the commission about the matter in order to verify the facts. The applicants for this position were orally examined by Mr. F. V. Moffatt, superintendent of Lights of the Department of Marine, Quebec, and the Reverend Brother Germain, Director-not janitor -of the Christian Brothers' Commercial school, Quebec, as the commission's representative and a representative of the Canadian Legion. It was a fairly good body of examiners, as the result shows. What was the result? The applicants were rated on their experience, intelligence, personal qualifications and physical fitness, and as a result of the ratings Mr. J.	J. Kiley, a returned soldier with extensive experience as mechanic and fitter, was selected for the appointment and has been found by the department to be satisfactory in every way. A certificate in favour of this gentleman was furnished prior to the examination by Mr. B. J. Kaine, marine agent at Quebec.

That disposes of the pleasant little canard with reference to the janitor of St. Patrick's church or any other church in Quebec.
The hon. member also cast ridicule upon the present method of appointing postmasters and submitted-imagine an intelligent member of the house doing so!-that a member of a constituency is better fitted than the Civil Service Commission to appoint postmasters. What are the facts? We all know from our personal experience the pressure that is brought to bear upon us from every quarter. We know very well that sincere and hardworking individuals, meeting hard times, will come and say: Look here, Garland or Jones or Bennett, I am up against it; my crop has failed this year; my family is growing up; I have to have some money; I am tired of the farm anyway and I would like a job as a postmaster or a boiler mechanic or something else; cannot you get me into the service? The pressure is unrelenting, persistent under the patronage system. The average member has little idea of the qualifications required in a postmaster, and if he has the giving of the appointment will on many occasions give it to a friend without regard to his qualifications. But what is the position under the merit system? Let us say that under the merit system a vacancy has been created or has occurred. The position is advertised. The people in that district may apply. Applications are sent in. An examination is held by the post office inspector of the district. This gentleman is a man who has worked himself up in that branch of the civil service until his decisions are certainly entitled to be regarded as having some authority and weight. He gives the applicants a thorough examination in regard to the following qualifications:
1.	Training and experience.
2.	Personal qualifications.
3.	Standing in the community.
4.	The location and accommodation he is willing to offer for the post office.
The fourth is a technical qualification. The post office inspector then rates the applicants in the order of merit and submits the list to Ottawa. The Civil Service Commission then verifies the facts as set forth, especially with regard to qualifications and soldier preference, and having verified the facts, awards the position. That is an infinitely preferable situation for the sake of both the member himself and the whole service, to throwing the outside service, including postmasters, into the hands of the distributors of the old type of political patronage.
The method adopted by the Civil Service Commission in connection with outside

Civil Service Act-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
appointments, technical or otherwise, is to appoint a local examining board, one or more of whom shall be representative directly of the commission. For example, supposing an architect is required, let us say in Winnipeg. This is a technical position. What is done in such a case? A board is appointed consisting of a local architect, a man well known in his profession, the district architect of the Department of Public Works and a third architect. Such a board is certainly far more capable than a member of parliament to pass upon applications for a position of that kind.
I might not know the qualifications of an architect; in fact I am quite free to admit I would not. This bill takes no recognition of that; it would exclude the entire outside service from the Civil Service Commission and throw it once more into the hands of patronage. I wonder if hon. members know what that means? Before I tell them what it means, let me make this citation to the hon. member. He called in as witnesses on his behalf, but he did not show how they were witnesses, the Beique report and the Malcolm report. Both of these reports come out stubbornly and definitely for the merit system. The Beique report states:
Your committee is convinced that the method of appointment and promotion by competition (usually known as the merit system) is preferable. in every way, to advancement by favour or influence. In support of this principle may be cited the findings of a number of committees. extracts from which wall be found in the appendix to this report.
This bill is certainly not following out the Beique report in that regard. Then the Malcolm report has this to say:
Your committee is of the opinion that the two fundamental principles of the Civil Service Act are the merit system and the system of appointment by competitive examination, and that both these principles must be preserved.
Again I ask my hon. friend to substantiate his claim that this bill is modeled after either or both of these reports. It was a ridiculous assertion and had no foundation in fact. The passing of this bill would throw the whole civil service of Canada back to the period of 1908 and you would again have the same old struggle against the hordes of patronage until you established a worth while, businesslike civil service act. Do not let me be misunderstood. I believe there is incorrect administration of the present act; I am not satisfied with it. Sufficient has come to my attention in the last three or four years to convince me that the government is on the right track when it proposes a committee of investigation. But that is an entirely different thing from passing a bill to sabotage the entire merit
principle. I am utterly against the bill and am absolutely in favour of an investigation. This bill should be defeated and the committee appointed. We can then, as a result of the committee's findings, determine what amendments, if any, are necessary to the Civil Service Act, and what reorganization of the Civil Service Commission is necessary if a reorganized commission is decided upon.
Secondly, this bill will radically alter the whole method of promotion. It will leave in the hands of the ministers and deputy ministers-and in their hands alone, mark you -the whole power of promotion even within the inside service. Imagine what a hopeless position the whole service would be in if it is to be again subject to the miserable, petty, personal elements which prevailed for so many years before the Civil Service Act came into force.
Lastly, but among the most important of all considerations to which I direct the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite, the passing of this bill will almost completely destroy the effectiveness of the returned soldier preference in respect of at least thirty thousand positions. Why do I say that? This bill does not say that the returned soldier preference shall be abolished, but it does exclude from the operation of the Civil Service Act, under which the soldier preference has existed, the entire outside service, including also, by modification, the merit system with respect to the inside service. What has happened that would justify my statement that this would mean almost the entire destruction of the returned soldier preference? That is a point upon which I wish to dwell; for I am satisfied that no hon. gentleman opposite, on being acquainted with the facts and faced with the actual conditions that will arise, will support this bill. I therefore press this particular point upon them in view of their protestations in the past.
The Veteran, the official organ of the returned soldiers, some few years ago made an analysis into the operation of the soldier preference in respect of positions excluded from the operation of the act. Hon. members of this house who were here in past years will recollect that the late administration, much to its discredit and much to my disappointment and over my adverse vote and speech, did exclude from the operation of the Civil Service Act some 18.000 odd positions. More than that, 12,000 positions were excluded from the operation of the act in one order in council alone. The Veteran decided to make an examination, and they found out this, and

Civil Service Act-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
published it in the form of two tables. The first table shows the number of male appointments to the civil service by the Civil Service Commission for the years from 1920 to 1924, both inclusive, as follows:

So there you have a reduction from 53.97 per cent to 10.03 per cen-t. It is a fair contention, then, with the evidence in front of us, to state that this bill will largely destroy the effectiveness of the returned soldier preference.
When this bill was up the last time, I referred to the attitude of the Conservative party in regard thereto, much to its credit. The great battery of Conservatism for this bill was Sir Robert Borden, and to him stands the credit for having ultimately forced the issue in this house. I think it was in 1907 that he secured the acquiescence of the entire party in the Halifax platform, which included the following:
A thorough and complete reformation of the laws relating to the civil service, so that future appointments shall be made by an independent commission acting upon the report of examiners after competitive examination.
Speaking on that occasion he said:
I need not dwell on the importance of this. Of necessity some appointments must be left to the responsibility of the executive. Appointments to the judicial bench and certain other high public offices are of this character, and the people have it in their power to compel an honourable and decent performance of this great public duty. There are also many minor appointments which could not for the present be brought within such a system.

But for the rest, I prefer a competitive system of appointment to the present partisan system.
Three-fourths of the time of members supporting a government is occupied in dealing with matters of patronage. Party patronage and party service have more weight than character and capacity. The public service is cumbered with useless officials. I am convinced that we shall perform a great public duty by establishing in this country that system which prevails in Great Britain under which a member of parliament has practically no voice in or control over any appointment to the civil service.
That became the fixed policy of the Conservative party. Sir Robert Borden says that the Halifax platform became the policy of 'the Liberal-Conservative party, which was thus committed to the principle of civil service reform upon the lines above set forth.
Later on, not satisfied with the general announcement of the fact, the late Sir George Foster rose in the house in the year following, 1908, and moved the following resolution:
That the civil service system of Canada should be based on merit and character alone and all the appointments thereto should be made from candidates whose competency has been established through open competitive examinations conducted under a non-partisan civil service commission.
On that occasion Sir Robert Borden said:
I again repeated my conviction that appointments, both in the inside and outside service, should be based upon results obtained by competitive examination and that the system prevailing in Great Britain should be adopted in Canada.
So the issue was joined. But the battle continued, and Sir Robert Borden said that it was impossible to secure the passage of this effective legislation which we have in the Civil Service Act so long as only one party was in office. It was not until the Union government was formed in the war years that it became possible in 1918 to put over the act. Now only a few years later, comparatively speaking, we have the proposal from the Conservative ranks to destroy the splendid work of all the preceding years and to render almost impotent the Civil Service Act.

speechtext:
So long as the party system continues in this country it is essential for the character and efficiency of men in the public service that men of all political parties shall have nothing to say as to appointments to the civil service. Both appointments and promotions should depend upon the merit system, should depend solely upon the merit and capacity of the candidates who offer themselves. If I had the time at my disposal I could continue quoting from the eloquent speeches of the great leaders of the Conservative party. Right Hon. Arthur Meighen made some of the most pronounced and courageous statements in regard to the maintenance of the merit system. The present Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) made an eloquent plea in support of the merit system. The right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) no later than 1928 made an eloquent speech on the same subject. Speaking in this house on May 8, 1928, he said:
It-
Referring to a resolution aimed against the act.
-means the recurrence of the patronage system, which should not be tolerated in this country. It is not conducive to good service or to the public weal. While there have been many defects in connection with the administration of the civil service the fact is that it is a great advance over anything we have had heretofore in this country. We protest, against any effort being made to return to the old condition of patronage.
I echo his words to-day and protest against any attempt, either through private bill, resolution or committee of this house, to return to the old days of patronage.
Not content with that, the Prime Minister -of course at that time he was not Prime Minister-speaking on May 16, 1928, is reported at page 3221 of Hansard as follows:
I do not propose to trespass upon the time of the house further than to say that it is essential that we should maintain in its integrity the principle of appointments to office being made by the Civil Service Commission.
Could anything be clearer or more sharply defined than that? The present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) is reported at page 3169 of Hansard as follows:
Undoubtedly the patronage system had more evil attached to it than merit. Appointments under the patronage system are made for the purpose-I think I can put it simply and plainly -of giving jobs to those who are in favour of the ministry of the day, whatever ministry it is. ... I am opposed to this bill to the extent that it departs from the principle of appointment by the Civil Service Commission.
I think it is only fair to give the statement, one which is certainly well worth
giving, of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion). Hansard of May 15, 1928, at page 3173, contains the following:
Because of this strong public opinion in favour of the merit system under the Civil Service Commission, I think the minister should hesitate long before going back to a system which, rightly or wrongly, has become discredited. On the whole I believe the Civil Service Commission have given the country reasonably satisfactory service, and whatever faults they may have-and no doubt no commission is perfect-those faults are few and slight compared with the condition of affairs under the old system.
I thoroughly agree with the minister's statement, and sincerely hope his views have not changed since then. I hope he and his colleagues, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Prime Minister, and his colleague in the Senate, the leader of that respectable body, will reject utterly the proposal of the hon. member for Dorchester.
Again, time limits me; had I time I could quote resolutions piling in to myself and other members opposed to this bill, coming from every branch of the civil service in the Dominion of Canada. I could quote reports of commissions and committees which have been appointed within the last fifteen or twenty years, every one of which was opposed to the very principle embodied in this bill. Mr. Speaker, if this house does itself justice -justice not only to its own conscience and intelligence, but to the cause of the civil sendee in general-it will reject the bill. I purpose voting against it.
