Mr. Speaker, the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Ca'han) mentioned my name as one member to sit on a committee which, among its other duties, would have to consider this bill. At once the house must recognize the very difficult position in which other members of that committee and myself are placed. According to the interpretation of the rules of the house, if I vote for the second reading of this bill I shall have committed myself to the principle of it. If I vote against the second reading and the second reading should carry and the bill be referred to the committee of which I am a member, I should be placed in the same embarrassing position. Therefore at this stage I cannot address my remarks to the merits, if any, or the demerits of the bill now before the house. I may add, however, that if ever there was a bill-I do not think I am saying too much-which should have been used for the purpose of establishing the precedent which was established yesterday, this is the bill.

Civil Service Act-Mr. Heaps
Mr. A, A. HEAPS (North Winnipeg): Mr. Speaker, I should like to make one or two observations concerning the bill now before the house. I believe every member ought to be in favour of maintaining an efficient civil service. The question arises as to how we are likely to effect that end which, I think, ought to be the object of every member of parliament. In my view it is impossible to have an efficient civil service if we revert to a system of patronage and fill vacancies in the civil service at the request or bidding of members. Consequently I feel constrained to oppose the measure now before the house.
At this time I am wondering who is asking for the change outlined by the bill. I have yet to find from any source whatsoever any indication as to who is seeking these changes. I do know, however, that from many sources throughout the length and breadth of Canada there is a strong feeling of resentment and opposition to this measure.
I am one who believes in the merit system; I realize fully that the moment patronage creeps into the system of appointments merit goes by the board. I believe employers and employees recognize that in the filling of vacancies there are two principles to be maintained, namely merit and seniority. In all my experiences as a public representative I have always attempted, when I have had to deal with the filling of vacancies, to be guided by those two factors. As a rule one does not go far astray if he observes those principles. On more than one occasion when I stood as a , candidate for public office I have taken the stand that I refused to act as an employment agent for my constituents. I have refused to approach department heads asking for employment for those who happened to be within the boundaries of my constituency. I am of opinion that from a political point of view, the handling of patronage by members of the house does far more harm than good. The obtaining of a few privileges for a constituent does not necessarily make friends for a member. I have found that members who have been able to obtain positions for a favoured few have, as a result of their activities, made more enemies than friends.
One of the chief reasons which has prompted me to rise in my place this evening was a statement made by the hon. member who introduced this measure to the house. He said he would like to have an extension of the patronage now existing, and made reference to the appointment of postmasters as one reason for a change in the Civil Service Act. I have not had as long an experience in
[Mr. <~!hevrier.J
this house as have some other hon. members. One incident however came under my observation to which at this time I feel constrained to refer. The hon. member who introduced the measure urged that if appointments were left to the discretion of hon. members of the house-which, of course, would mean hon. members on the government side-better appointments would1 be the result. To-night there occurs to my mind one appointment which was made and to which I shall make special reference at this juncture. Through a vacancy which occurred in the city of Winnipeg an appointment was recommended by a member of the party in power. For obvious reasons I shall not refer to any names. I learned that a certain gentleman was to be appointed to a responsible position, and to my amazement I was informed that the recommendation made by a Conservative, was in favour of a man who 'had a criminal record and whose family's record was no better than his own. This man was actually recommended for a responsible position.

No, it did not. I should like to amend the act so that we may obviate things of this character. To my astonishment the appointment was made, although people in the district had signed a petition in protest and transmitted it to the minister, and I myself protested emphatically the objectionable nature of the appointment. I told the parties responsible for the appointment, "I do not mind your appointing a Conservative to the office, I expect you to do it, but in the name of decency and common sense appoint an honest Conservative."
May I point out further that the individual so appointed was handling His Majesty's mail. A few days after the appointment his son was released from the penitentiary, and very soon afterwards complaints came from my constituents that this person was also handling the mail. I protested to the responsible minister, but I could not make the slightest impression. Later when I came to Ottawa I called on him and told him that unless something was done to cancel the appointment I would feel obliged to raise the matter on the floor of the house when his estimates were under consideration. Then I received a promise that action would be taken. What happened? On the first of October last a change was made-the daughter was put in her father's place. Now the house is being requested by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) to extend the patronage system in order that we may get a

Civil Service Act-Mr. Bourassa
more efficient civil service! At the time the protest to which I have referred was being made against the appointment the chief of police of Winnipeg was asked for the man's record; this was submitted to the minister but nothing could be done to cancel the appointment. I said to the local postmaster, "Go down to the police station and make inquiries in regard to the character of this man." He did so, and was told, "That man's reputation stinks to the sky." Yet he was appointed to this responsible position in the city.
We have been told by the mover of this bill that the Civil Service Commission is at the bar of public opinion. Nothing of the kind, Mr. Speaker. What is now at the bar of public opinion is the action of members of this house in regard to this bill. Are we going to return to the patronage system, or shall we put more power into the hands of the Civil Service Commission. If the personnel of the commission is unsatisfactory, then it does not seem to me that we have to repeal the act; the logical thing to do is to change the personnel so that any defects of the commission may be remedied.
I move, seconded by Mr. Coote:
That the word "now" be left out, and the words "this day six months" added at the end of the question.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there seems to be a certain confusion between the administration of the Civil Service Act by the Civil Service Commission and the object of this bill. That reform should be made in the operation of the act and perhaps certain amendments incorporated in order to make it more effective I think is conceded on all sides. But to adopt the principle of this bill and revert to the old patronage system would be a step backward that would stamp the parliament of Canada very unfavourably in the eyes of all civilized nations that have reformed their civil service system. I know something of the operation of the civil service in England, and I think there is unanimity of opinion among all public men there as well as among all other people that civil service reform has been one of the greatest political and administrative reforms adopted in that country in the last century.
With regard to the outside service, the withdrawal of which from the Civil Service Commission is the main object of this bill, to a certain extent I agree with the member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon). No doubt the idea of giving, theoretically,-I insist on the word and I am going to explain its application -of giving, theoretically, authority to three gentlemen in Ottawa to make appointments to
every petty office, such as the postmastership in a small village or the caretakership of a small public building, is preposterous, because they have to rely upon somebody to advise them; and that is what they do. The idea that these three gentlemen could always appoint the proper men to every small post office from Sydney to Prince Rupert is out of the question. But to say that these appointments should be handed back to members of parliament is something on which I cannot agree with my hon. friend. He says that the member representing the constituency is better informed than any other man with regard to the qualifications of persons for such appointments. Well, if by that he means any member representing a constituency it may be so. But then is he prepared to recommend to the government, and are his friends who uphold his views ready to recommend to any government, that they take the advice of every member of the house, to whatever party he belongs, to the same degree as they would take the advice of their own friends? Maybe he could secure such a promise verbally, but human nature being what it is, he knows very well that in every constituency represented by an independent or an opposition member there would be an uproar among his own supporters if that promise were redeemed; they would complain that the patronage was in the hands of the opposition. I have found that to be the case time and again. I will not insist on that aspect of the question.
The suggestion I make is this. I think all those who would stick to the principle of the Civil Service Act, who think that we should not. revert to the evil of patronage, should vote against the bill. But at the same time that does not prevent the committee proposed by the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) going into all the aspects of the situation, and if they think proper, they might recommend certain amendments to the act in order to give an opportunity in every constituency for people at large, municipal councillors or others, to advise the responsible heads of the department in the appointment of petty officers. I would have no objection to that. Certainly some changes should be made.
May I say in that regard that the patronage system has not proven effective, even from the point of view of my hon. friend. Take the narrow point of view as stated by the hon.
' member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps)- and that is very old history-members of parliament have suffered much more by the exercise of patronage than they have gained from it. Naturally when they have just won an election they feel the elation of victory, and
464	COMMONS
Civil Service Act-Mr. Kennedy (Winnipeg)
they like to show a little of the spirit of domination in their county; but that does not last long. As was stated by Mr. Louis Frechette, the poet-he was a- member of parliament for a short time-for every appointment recommended by him to the government he made one ungrateful person and a hundred others furious against him. He never gained anything thereby. But that is a small aspect of the question.
From the purely administrative point of view my opinion is that much more authority and freedom of action should be left to the permanent heads of departments, not to the ministers. I think ministers themselves are much too bothered with questions of patronage as it is. They should have enough confidence in their deputy ministers and the heads of the various branches of their departments to rely upon them in all that concerns promotions and appointments from a list prepared by the Civil Service Commission, based on the technical merits of the candidates.
That is with regard to the inside service. As far as the outside service is concerned I may tell the house that the method I generally adopted, even in the old days, was to inquire from the people of the community which place was best suited for a post office, and what person was most capable of rendering service to the people. I recommended the person designated by the people of the community, without regard to politics. I would find it hard to say, of all the recommendations I have made, whether they concerned Liberals or Conservatives, for the very good reason that most of them vote for me no matter what may be their politics.
However that is beside the question. I repeat that a greater opportunity should be given the people concerned in local appointments to express their views, and those views should be accepted by the department. Much more responsibility should be given the permanent heads of departments, just as in large corporations like the Canadian Pacific railway, the president and board of directors do not concern themselves all the time with the appointment of employees. They rely upon certain responsible heads of various departments to choose their employees according to their requirements, and the employees are promoted gradually under the two standards indicated by the hon. member for North Winnipeg, that is, seniority and merit. Then they are largely protected through their labour organizations. Now that the civil service has organized itself on a proper basis, some suggestions of that kind might be studied by the committee, and I think the object of my good 
friend from Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) might be served. I know him well enough to be sure that his object is not simply to exercise political patronage. Then the committee could report to the house and the house might take action, of course under the guidance of the government, without having to accept the principle of this bill to which, for my part, I am utterly opposed.

Mr. Speaker, the time available for the discussion of this bill, scarcely five minutes, will hardly permit any detailed analysis, and I do not purpose to attempt to do so at this time. Lest the time elapse before I have an opportunity of stating my view of the bill I shall reverse the ordinary procedure and, before giving my reasons, state that I am opposed to the principle of the bill and I shall vote against it. It is with some regret that I find myself holding the view that I cannot support a bill introduced by my good friend and colleague the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon), but there is a principle involved of very wide application.
The bill divides itself into two parts. One provision is that all civil service appointments, outside of appointments at Ottawa, shall be removed from the operation of the Civil Service Act. As to the remainder, that is to say, the appointments to the service at Ottawa, even in those cases the right of the commission to make such appointments is very considerably curtailed.
With regard to outside appointments, if this bill were enacted as introduced, what would be the practical effect? It would then devolve upon the member for each constituency, with such advisers as he may gather around him in the way of an executive, to recommend from time to time persons to fill vacancies. It would not be complimentary to other hon. members of this house to urge that, from whatever constituency they may come, they would not use good judgment in such matters or that they would not be competent to make good selections. The dangers from that point of view would seem largely theoretical. I believe that an hon. member faced with the duty of recommending a person for any position in his constituency would be guided by the merit of the individual who might be recommended. It may be urged that it is only natural that a member would nominate someone from his own political party. Perhaps that is quite true, but as I am quite prepared to concede that a Liberal member repre-

Unemployment-Mr. Reid
senting a constituency can find among bis followers men worthy of being nominated for positions of honour and trust, so I think they will concede that we on this side of the house can find such men among our own supporters.
Therefore it is not primarily the question of appointments in respect to which I am apprehensive, but it is the effect upon the service itself. If the political be the first consideration in the matter of appointments, when you come to a change of government the supporters of the member then representing the constituency in question, remembering that certain appointments were made first because of political considerations, will demand, and press that demand with considerable force, that, the new government having the right to exercise discretion and make a change, the change be made. In very large measure the principle will apply that "those who live by the sword shall die by the sword."

When the house rose at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was telling of an incident that occurred in my own constituency in connection with patronage under relief work being carried on by the federal government. I was induced to refer to this because of the remarks of the Minister of Labour with regard to patronage in another district.
A grant of some S6.300 was made for the construction of a wharf at White Rock, and when I visited the job I found that the names of the men employed had been furnished by the district engineer. On making inquiries of the district engineer I was informed that he had been given these names by the Conservative association. Despite the fact that he had been notified, as hon. members were notified, that in all work carried on for the relief of unemployment, federal or otherwise, no discrimination was to be shown, he had deliberately gone to the Conservative organization and obtained the names of the men who were working on that federal relief job. On his own word he confessed it. I asked the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) to take serious note of this, because patronage may be bad enough in ordinary times but it becomes terrible in times of stress when only those be-41761-30
longing to the party are given a chance to participate in the grant.
I have just received another telegram from the municipality of Burnaby. I received one on Monday last and again to-day, and before quoting them I will state that they are contrary to the advice given to me by the department. I was told that in connection with the $2,500,000 sent to the province of British Columbia, vouchers would not be required to be O.K'd before payment was made to the municipalities. I transmitted that information to the municipality which immediately got in touch with Victoria, when the information was given that such was not the case. The telegram which I received on Monday reads as follows:
Total amount spent on direct relief to January 31, $65,844, total payment received to date, $32,681. Cost of direct relief shared equally by municipality, province and dominion under unemployment relief acts, 1930 and 1931.
The telegram continues:
Total expenditure on unemployment relief works, $341,000; total of vouchers already submitted to Victoria, $310,935. Total payments received to date, $132,125.
They were advised that Victoria was waiting for funds from Ottawa before paying out any money. The telegram I received to-day reads as follows:
McGeough advises that Victoria has received one million dollars. Phoned Deputy Minister of Finance at Victoria who states he can only pay provincial and municipality's share; is still awaiting authority from Ottawa to pay Dominion's share. Instructions received by Victoria forbid them to release Dominion's share till Ottawa passes the vouchered accounts and issues an order for payment. Believe this is the cause of conflicting reports. Payment will be held up indefinitely until this is cleared up.
I would direct the attention of the hon. Minister of Labour to the seriousness of this situation. As long as these conflicting reports exist, the buck will be passed from one government to the other and great distress will be caused to the municipalities. Conditions are somewhat similar in other districts. Last week I received a telegram from the city of Femie, in the constituency of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), advising that similar conditions exist there. Other municipalities are feeling the stress of this unemployment problem, and I would like to quote a portion of a telegram sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) on January 27. This telegram shows that the municipalities had an idea that the government had agreed to pay over the money as soon as the

Unemployment-Mr. Barber

agreements were signed by Hon. Senator Robertson. The telegram, in part, reads as follows:
We now find municipalities in desperate circumstances owing to work programs being curtailed so that now relief work has practically ceased and municipalities appear to have no alternative but direct relief. We now apply to you to have work relief programs as originally presented and agreed to by Senator Robertson put into force so that we can have work completed as therein laid out. To cease unemployment relief work at this time will not only cause hardship to unemployed but will be uneconomical as many works would be left unfinished. We are distinctly opposed to spending municipal moneys on direct relief as no returns to taxpayers accrue. Other municipalities not included in previous work programs have to care for local cases and want some consideration given at this time to their requirements, and to make conditions worse, provincial road work has ceased. Municipal taxpayers are in no position to finance any undertakings to take care of these situations as the ability of taxpayers to pay was fully demonstrated last year when in many municipalities only sixty per cent of 1931 tax levy was paid. Any additional increase will mean many will lose their home.

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to take part in this debate until the last speaker, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) wandered away from his own district and encroached upon one of my municipalities. Speaking in support of this motion of want of confidence in the government, the hon. member cited the case of a political friend of his, the reeve of a municipality in his district, who has had some trouble in obtaining assistance in the matter of unemployment relief from both the federal and provincial governments. I listened carefully for forty minutes to the hon. gentleman, and after hearing him read many letters and telegrams I came to the conclusion that this was entirely a misunderstanding. The hon. member mentioned a municipality in Fraser Valley constituency and referred to it as being in the same plight as this almost notorious place, Burnaby, of which we have been hearing so much this session. I have received a letter from the reeve of Coquitlam, in which he draws to my attention some trouble which he had had but which proved to be a misunderstanding. This letter is addressed to me, and the first two paragraphs read as follows:
As a result of a meeting with the hon. Mr. Bruhn,-
Mr. Bruhn is the Minister of Public Works in the provincial government. The letter continues:
-at his room in the Vancouver hotel at the time of the visit of the Hon. G. Robertson,

federal Minister of Labour, I was made to understand that our municipal proposal under the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act, 1931, amounting to $34,800 would meet with approval on the basis of 50 per cent federal contribution, including labour and material, and 25 per cent provincial contribution for labour only.
On the strength of this verbal assurance we submitted a money by-law to our ratepayers for the balance, for their approval.
I took up this matter with Mr. Hereford, the dominion director, and his letter in reply explains this case. It is addressed to myself and reads:
I am directed by the Minister of Labour to acknowledge yours of February 10 regarding unemployment relief matters for the district of Coquitlam.
The agreement with the province provides for an expenditure of $19,000 for Coquitlam to which the Dominion government contributes 50 per cent.
With regard to the reeve's statement that at the time of the visit of the Hon. Senator Robertson to Vancouver, the reeve was made to understand that the amount which the Dominion government would contribute would be $34,800, I am quite satisfied that the Senator did not intend to convey any such impression as the Senator knew quite well and invariably stated that all submissions were subject to the approval of council.
The undersigned accompanied Senator Robertson on his trip to British Columbia last summer and I have been present during hundreds of interviews, both at Ottawa and all over Canada, and observed that the Senator invariably made it clear that however much he might personally favour a proposal, and however far he was whiling to go in recommending it to the government, it was always subject to the approval of council. The financial situation as it exists in British Columbia and other provinces is not what we would desire. The finances of our province as well as that of others, of the dominion as a whole and of other countries, have been adversely affected by the worldwide economic depression. The people of British Columbia will agree that the present financial troubles in that province do not all lie at the door of the Conservative party. Before
going into details of the administration of the unemployment relief money in the province of New Brunswick and especially in the county I have the honour to represent, I wish to refer briefly to the speech made this afternoon by the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon). I note that he claimed that the unemployment relief system as now admin-

istered has proved a huge success, and he quoted figures to show that some three million days' work had been given to the unemployed in Canada. He gave the number of unemployed receiving the opportunity of doing this relief work as 300,000 odd. But if we dissect those figures, Mr. Speaker, we will find that they mean on an average 23 days' work for
300.000	or 350,000 unemployed, or if you place it on a yearly basis of employment, it means the giving of work to only 25,000 out of
350.000	unemployed, and that at a cost of $70,000,000 to the Dominion of Canada, to the provinces, to the municipalities and to the two railways which took part in providing unemployment relief work. If that is a huge success in administering unemployment relief under the act that was passed in September, 1930, then I would like to know what success really means in that line.
Having dealt with that phase of the minister's argument let me now refer to other parts of his speech. He produced evidence in an attempt to prove that the ex-Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) *was not telling the truth in connection with the administration of the unemployment relief fund in northern Ontario. But if you will carefully examine the proof, Mr. Speaker, which the hon. gentleman produced you will find that it was all negative evidence. Not one individual could the minister produce of his own personal knowledge to prove the contrary of that which the ex-Minister of Labour had alleged in this house. I was astonished to think that a gentleman occupying the position which the Minister of Labour does at the bar could find no other evidence but negative evidence to substantiate his refutation of the charges made by the ex-Minister of Labour. Negative evidence has no weight in court, and it should have no weight in parliament. The strongest proof that the minister could produce in refutation of what the ex-Minister of Labour had stated was quotations from a newspaper, the editor of which was a defeated Conservative candidate in the last provincial election in Ontario, and of course, being a Conservative attempting to defend a Conservative administration at Ottawa he would not be in any way biased; we can readily understand that. The attempt made by the minister to belittle the ex-Minister of Labour and to lessen the force of the charges of mismanagement of the situation by quoting the evidence to which I have just referred will not in any way lessen the esteem in which my colleague the ex-Minister of Labour is held by every workingman in this dominion. I think the Minister of Labour should have hesitated before

Unemployment-Mr. Veniot
violating the rules of the house in quoting from newspapers in an attempt to prove that statements made by an hon. member on the floor of this house were not in accordance with the truth. But he was so far lost for argument that he had to violate the rules in his attempt to prove that the ex-Minister had not stated to the house the facts as they were.
Let me now deal in some detail with the administration of the unemployment relief fund in the count}' which I have the honour to represent. I shall discuss that question under two heads: first, the expenditure of public money for unemployment relief purposes under the federal Minister of Public Works; second, the expenditure of unemployment relief money in cooperation with the provincial authorities in New Brunswick.
In taking up the first division of the subject, the expenditure of relief money under the direct supervision of the Minister of Public Works, I wish here publicly to pay my compliments to him and to thank him for the interest he displayed when complaints were laid before him as to the manner in which public money was being expended in the county of Gloucester. I want to thank him for the very determined stand he took when those complaints were laid before him to see that there would be no political discrimination, to see that those who got the money were really in need of it and that it would not be earned in the county of Gloucester by men who had bank accounts and did not require relief work to see them through the hardships of the winter.
On the 24th of October last year I happened to be in Ottawa. Previous to that I had visited certain of the works being carried on in my county, and after seeing the work I came to the minister and made my complaints. Why was I prompted to make those complaints? Because from personal investigation and personal knowledge I learned that the money voted by this parliament to be expended under the direct supervision of the federal Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) to help the unemployment situation was not being expended in the manner the minister and the government had promised.
I found that not only was the foreman of work at Grande Anse employed on the work but his two sons *were working also. Within a gun-shot of where he and his two sons were working, unemployed were crying out for bread for their families, and could get nothing. When applications were made to that man by unemployed men who had nothing in their houses for their families to
eat, his answer was, "You are on the wrong side of politics." I came here and complained to the Minister of Public Works, and as a result he issued from his office instructions to the district engineer in St. John to proceed not only to Grande Anse but to Petit Rodher and Caraquet, concerning all of which I had complained. Instructions were issued to the foremen in charge at those places that if they did not carry out the directions of the department they would be dismissed. A government engineer investigated and found that as far as Grande Anse was concerned my representations were well grounded. After his visit to Grande Anse conditions changed and those men who were not entitled to unemployment relief were put off the work and replaced by men in dire need of means to keep the wolf from the door.
The engineer was not as successful at Caraquet as he had been at Grande Anse. He visited Caraquet on Wednesday and found that wealthy fishermen, as the term goes ire that section of the country, men who had' money in the bank, were employed on relief work. He found that not one man working" on the Caraquet wharf needed unemployment relief to keep him through the winter, but men who lived from hand to mouth had! been refused work. The foreman promised that on the following Monday he would make a change, and would endeavour to comply with the regulations or instructions issued by the minister through the engineer. Monday arrived, but no change was made; Tuesday came and passed; Wednesday came and passed and no change was made. I reported the matter to the district engineer, who sent his assistant to Caraquet and found that the superintendent in charge was not carrying out instructions. As a result work was stopped, dismissals were made and the instructions of the minister complied with, when work was resumed. At this time I wish to thank the federal Minister of Public Works for his action.

I state from my place in
this house and on my honour as a member that in the county of Gloucester the unemployment relief money during the progress of a by-election was made the greatest campaign fund which possibly could be used in any county.
I make that statement advisedly; I am prepared to stand by it, and if the government chooses to appoint a federal commission I shall be able to bring before such commission evidence to substantiate every word I have said.
I made complaints to the Minister of Labour, and on September 30, 1931, I received the following letter from Mr. Harry Hereford, the Dominion Director of Unemployment Relief:
In the absence of the Minister of Labour from Ottawa on official business. I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of September 24, in which you complain regarding political discrimination in connection with work being carried out on provincial highway near your home.
I have investigated this matter so far as I was able to with the details you furnished, and I am advised by the provincial authorities that an individual was appointed at Bathurst to (Mr. Veniot.1
register the unemployed. This individual worked in conjunction with the Poor Commissioner who is appointed, as you are no doubt aware, through the county council, and that the same method is being followed in Northumberland,-
I do not know why he referred to Northumberland.
-and assurance is given that those needing employment most have been given work regardless of political or religious affiliation.
Who was the gentleman appointed to register the unemployed in the municipality of Gloucester? He was a man living in the town of Bathurst, having an office in an incorporated town which had nothing to do with a matter of unemployment relief. No man could enter the office for registration without having to take part in a discussion of the political situation. As to whether or not the individual received work depended greatly upon his comments along political lines.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Does the
hon. member know that of his own knowledge?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: You know a lot about Ontario, too.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
I know nothing about
Ontario, and I am only mentioning Ontario in reply to the interjections of my hon. friend -and I think I know enough about him to qualify those interjections as they should be. Now, sir, let me go one step further. On October 16 I sent this night message:
To Hon. Gideon Robertson,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa.
Doctor W. H. Coffyn, provincial government candidate in by-election now being held in Gloucester county publishes a call to the electors in which he makes the pretence that registration for unemployment relief comes through him as the government candidate. Speakers on government side do not hesitate to tell our people that the amount of relief money to be expended in this county depends upon the election of Dr. Coffyn. In many cases relief money is being earned by people who do not need it, and many who do need it badly are left in the cold. Relief money is being utilized as a vote getter and not as relief, and therefore I feel it my duty to enter a strong protest. The election takes place October twenty-sixth. A dirty canvass is being used that if Coffyn is defeated the relief work will be stopped. Has he any authority by which he can have relief work stopped in this county. Please wire me reply.

Unemployment-Mr. Veniot

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman who sent the telegram?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Oh!

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I knew the truth of what I was saying, every bit of it. I got no reply to that telegram one way or the other. What happened? On the first day of December-

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order that the same privilege of debating this question may be accorded to me as to other members,
I ask that you take the necessary action to establish peace and order, perhaps by expelling some of these members.

speakeroldname: The ACTING SPEAKER (Mr. MacDonald, Cape Breton South):
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Now, sir, I received no
further word from the Minister of Labour until December 1, 1930. On that day there arrived in Bathurst two gentlemen, Mr. J. B. Carter and Mr. Trottier. They called on me at three o'clock in the afternoon and told me they had been instructed by the Minister of Labour to proceed to Gloucester county and investigate the relief work that had been carried on in that county, based on complaints that I had sent to the minister. I said to Mr. Carter, "It would have been far better had the minister sent you at the time I made the complaints. Then you would have found the people at work against whom I complained in my telegrams and letters, and you would have had first hand information." "Well," he said, "they did not send me then; I am here now." I went to my home and compiled five pages of complaints and submitted the original -this is a copy-to Mr. Carter. He undertook to investigate the complaints. He was some eight or nine days in the county of Gloucester. What was the result of his investigation? I asked that his report be placed on the table of the house. Here is what I received as that report:
Memorandum to Dominion Director
In reference to attached newspaper clipping,-
I want the house to note those words, "newspaper clipping."
-you will note that the Honourable P. J. Veniot is reported as saying "At a place six miles from his home," he said, "twelve men with money in the bank were employed under the unemployment relief scheme, and riding back and forth in cars, not one of which cost less than $1,200."
Then he goes on to say that he investigated this and he did find that cars were being used by these gentlemen-gentlemen labourerswhite collar workmen, men who although they had money in the bank were taking a bite from the mouths of starving children in the vicinity for the sake of making $2 to add to their bank account. But the curious thing about the whole business is that at the end he says:
This work was not paid for under the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act, 1931.
Then why did he investigate?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Because you asked
him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I did not ask him to investigate. If he chose to take a newspaper clipping and act upon it, and then found that this was not unemployment relief work, what right had he to make that report to the minister? Why did he not report on my complaints with respect to the work on the old Bathurst road leading from East Bathurst for five miles out towards Chatham? Why did he not report on the investigation he made of the unemployment work in the parishes of New Bandon, Bathurst and Beresford? He investigated those. He had the evidence of thirty or forty people before him. Why did he not submit a report of those cases to the minister? That is why he was sent down to Gloucester county. Moreover, in my presence-and there is no mention of it in his report-in reply to the question: How was it that work done in the month of October had not yet been paid for on the fourth day of December?-one of the district engineers replied that the pay sheets were being held up because there were irregularities in them. The engineer under investigation had to admit that on the 26th of October there had been placed on the pay sheets relating to the East Bathurst road and South Bathurst road no less than two hundred names of men that never worked a minute on the 26th day of October. Mr. Carter has that evidence in his possession. Why did he not report it to the minister?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE

gentleman does not know what he is talking about. I have here, sir, in my possession, the returns from the Department of Labour submitted by the hon. minister three or four

Unemployment-Mr. Veniot
days ago. I find in 1930-31 there was no less than $47,000 of federal aid, besides the $47,000 of provincial aid, expended on roads and bridges in the county of Gloucester. If what Mr. Carter says is true, that this is all provincial work, then this document is false.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE

'This document must be
false because that money was spent in the county of Gloucester. The hon. Minister of Labour accepted the projects as they were submitted and the money was paid to the province of New Brunswick. There was over $750,000 worth of projects accepted by the Minister of Labour for the whole of New Brunswick. Of that amount something like $50,000 was to be spent on roads and bridges in the county of Gloucester. I saw the instructions which listed the work on the East Bathurst road as unemployment relief work under federal cooperation, so I know what I am talking about.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines

One more question and I
am through. How much money was spent on the East Bathurst road?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I cannot say, but I do know that part of the money spent for unemployment relief in Gloucester, with the cooperation of the federal and provincial governments, was spent on the East Bathurst road. Mr. Carter investigated an irregularity in the pay sheet, and on October 26, the day of the election, he found that not one man on that pay sheet had worked one minute. I know that because I stood at the poll where at least 125 of them voted.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
What sort of
people have you down there?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
They are no worse than
the grafters in your province, and heaven knows there are enough of them.
Now let us go on. Part of the unemployment relief money was spent at Blue Cove, and not only was part of that money used politically during a provincial election, but certain candidates for municipal honours who were supervisors of roads used the influence of that money to help their election to the municipal council.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
What is
wrong with that?

speechtext: Is that in New Brunswick, where a man earns that much?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Yes, it is in New Brunswick, and the same thing has happened in other parts of the dominion. Here is the case of another boy seventeen years of age whose father is employed the year round as a railway man. Here is the case of two sons of a foreman earning so much a day on the work, while the father earns $4.50 per day himself. Here is a case where the father is a carpenter on the work and the son is employed also.
