speechtext:
Have you the
names?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Yes, I have.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Give them to us.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
No, I will not. If an investigation is ordered I will give the names then.
I could go on at much greater length, sir, but in conclusion let me say that the statements I have made to the house regarding federal public works have been borne out by the resident engineer for the province of New Brunswick, and again I want to thank the Minister of Public Works for the attention he gave those complaints and the method he adopted to rectify matters. I say now, however, that Mr. Carter did investigate work that was done through the cooperation of both governments, and that he has the evidence of the padding of pay sheets on October 26, which affected 200 men who never did a tap of work. Further than that, I have it from Mr. Carter himself, and he showed me a list of names which he had gathered during his tour in Northumberland. His investigation in Gloucester county disclosed that the work slips which each man had signed contained names which had no right to be there because the individuals were not in need of unemployment relief. He told me that he would report the matter to the minister and have those names struck off the pay sheets and that the province would have to assume entire responsibility for the payment of those amounts. When I asked that that report be laid upon the table of this house I was told that the work was not unemployment relief work. Why did
Mr. Carter make that report if it was not in connection with unemployment relief? Why did he go and take photographs of the cars? Why did he obtain evidence as to the age of those cars? It was for one reason, and I hate to suspect that reason. The hon. minister attempted to belittle the member for Gloucester who was attempting to defend not only his own people but the government of Canada. I pointed out that the act passed by this house was being violated; why did they send Mr. Carter down there if it was not intended that this matter should be investigated?
These are the conditions as they exist in the county of Gloucester. When replying to the former Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) this afternoon, I was surprised the minister did not tell the house that he knew the scheme had not worked well, that the system had not brought about the results which had been anticipated. With that knowledge within his breast, I was surprised that he did not take the house into his confidence and state what steps the government would take this session to remedy the situation. A statement of that nature would have carried more weight in the country than the attempt he made to belittle the former Minister of Labour.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would not attempt to take up the time of this house in a discussion of this question were it not for the speech just delivered by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot).

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: The hon. .member always mentions me.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
There has been much ado about nothing. I am going to take the house into my confidence and state the truth of the matter.
On October 26 last there was a provincial by-election in the hon. member's county, and for the first time in twenty years he was trimmed, and trimmed to a frazzle. That is why he has attempted to-night to explode the bile which has been gathering in his system ever since that election. After what he has said about his own fellow citizens and his own electors I feel that someone should rise in his place in this house to defend the reputation of the people of the fair county of Gloucester. I do not believe they are nearly as bad as the hon. gentleman would have, this house and the country believe. If they are bad, it is because of the tutoring they have received from the hon. member for Gloucester.
I have some knowledge of the unemployment relief situation in the province of New
474	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Hanson (Sunbury)
Brunswick. I have taken special interest in this work in my own constituency, where, I am glad to say, the condition is not quite as bad as prevails in other parts of the province. I happen to know that in connection with the expenditure of unemployment relief moneys in the province of New Brunswick, the Deputy Minister of Public Works, under whose immediate caire the expenditure takes place, has issued specific instructions that unemployment relief is to be granted without regard to politics, race, creed or religion. Those are the instructions sent out in the signed manual of the Deputy Minister of Public Works, and I know they have been observed to the letter in the constituency of York-Sunbury. The hon. gentleman will not find one single complaint of the administration of the unemployment relief fund in my constituency, and this applies to direct relief and the relief granted by the municipalities in cooperation with the provincial government.
I do not pretend to have any first-hand knowledge of the situation in the county of Gloucester, but if the truth were known I have just as much first-hand information as has the hon. gentleman. I venture to state that ninety-nine per cent of the assertions which he has made to-night are based on hearsay evidence. In the very nature of the cases themselves it could not possibly be otherwise.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: It was a personal investigation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
If what
somebody else told the hon. gentleman is not hearsay evidence, then I do not know what is hearsay evidence.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I saw the work being carried on and I know of individuals who had no right to be working.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
That may be true; there may have been men there that should not have been employed, but I am not in a position, nor is the hon. gentleman, to say whether this or that man has a bank account. If he is in a position to state that, then he is sticking his nose into somebody else's business, something which he has no right to do.
With respect to the specific complaints made to the department by the hon. member for Gloucester, he admits that as soon as those complaints were made, and because they were made by him as the member for Gloucester, they were immediately investigated. The information I have received from the authorities in the province of New Brunswick is that in all these cases the works being carried on 
were not unemployment relief works conducted by the province and the dominion jointly, but were purely provincial works. What right has this government to investigate such works? I say to my hon. friend in all kindness, he is in the wrong court. If he has the courage of his convictions, he will have some of his henchmen from the county of Gloucester lay a charge and stake their seats in the provincial legislature.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: They are going to.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I venture to say that not one of them has the courage to lay a charge and stake his seat on the outcome.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Did they not do it last
winter?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I thought the hon. member did not like interruptions.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
My mind
goes back to 1919 when the hon. gentleman was Minister of Public Works in the provincial government, and when the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Smith) was a member of the provincial legislature. The latter hon. gentleman laid charges with respect to the Shippigan road, and an investigation was held. Charges were laid in connection with the administration of public moneys in respect to this road in the county of Gloucester, and who do you suppose held the investigation? The Minister of Public Works. That is the method he adopted when he was Minister of Public works, and I should like to contrast it with the method adopted by this government. The investigation disclosed that there were boys of twelve years of age who were on the payroll and drawing a man's pay. There was one child of eight years drawing a man's pay. That is not denied; in fact, it never was denied. I was present at the investigation and the hon. member did not take any part in the hearing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Because I had no right.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
That is the fact. I never made any fuss about it because the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton was present, and he was quite capable of carrying on the investigation.
With these few observations I should like to conclude by saying this, that in New Brunswick, so far as I have 'any knowledge, either personal or by hearsay, there has been an economical expenditure of the public moneys under the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act. I have personal knowledge of the direct expenditure that was made by the Dominion government through the public

Unemployment-Mr. Bradette
works engineer, and I venture to say that not a dollar of that was wasted and that it went where it was most needed. That is what we on this side of the house undertook to do so far as it was humanly possible. I believe that has been done in the majority of cases and I would hate to think the fair county of Gloucester was any exception.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is my duty
to speak on this matter of unemployment in order to give at least the viewpoint of the riding which I have the honour to represent.
I was astonished at the reply given by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) and at the attitude he has taken in bringing into the political field this question which is a matter of importance to Canada as a whole. It is not my intention to defend the actions of the ex-Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan), but I believe they do not need any defence; they were judged by the country as a whole during the five years he was in office. The regulations that he has been instrumental in having passed in regard to labour questions will be remembered for many years to come by our Canadian workmen. I might also mention that by his constructive criticism he has been helpful in remedying the bad situation that existed in northern Ontario in previous years, and he should be given praise by the labour men of northern Ontario for bettering their living conditions. I appreciate the love the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) has for northern Ontario and his faith in that section of the country, but I believe the settlers and all the citizens there love that district; they make it their home, they believe in its future. But again let me state that to the constructive criticism that was made on the hustings and in this house by the ex-Minister of Labour, and even in the Ontario legislature, is due the better accommodation afforded to the men working on the trans-Canada highway in northern Ontario.
I do not wish to open up old sores, but I have clearly in mind, and I believe the people of northern Ontario as a whole remember very distinctly, the words that were uttered by the leaders of the Conservative party during the last general election. Their motto was: What Canada needs is a policy that will provide jobs. The majority of the people believed that statement. The Conservative leaders told the people in northern Ontario most emphatically that if the Liberals were put out of power and the Conservatives elected in their place, they would find work overnight. I am not going to fight all the old battles, but I wish to bring this question up from
another angle, so as to make my point clear. In the dying hours of last session we gave the present government a blank cheque as a result of which the people of Canada as a whole expected that there would be no more unemployment throughout the country. During the whole of last summer ministers o! the Ontario cabinet and of the federal government went up and down the country telling the people that every man who was unemployed would find employment at once.
I am no sob sister, but I must say that in the section which I represent there are many people who are still unemployed and a great number who are near to starvation. The Minister of Labour said this afternoon that there was no starvation in Canada. There is a great difference between prosperity and enjoyment of the ordinary comforts of life. He knows that section of the country and in the rural districts settlers who came in there fifteen or twenty years ago are to-day receiving S7.20 per week. They find it impossible at that wage to have the comforts of life to which they are entitled. I mention these facts because again I must say very sincerely I regret the attitude of the Minister of Labour in his opening remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: When the hon. member was in northern Ontario first, about fifteen or twenty years ago, did he have the comforts of life that he now has?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Fl'teen or twenty years ago we were certainly more prosperous than we are to-day. The situation is not getting any better; in fact, it is getting worse.
The Minister of Labour mentioned the question of patronage. We have suffered from patronage in northern Ontario in the past; indeed, I and my family have suffered from it. But because we aroused public sentiment and educated the people to realize that there was no such thing as Liberal or Conservative money; that every settler and every citizen in our section, whether Conservative or Liberal, was entitled to get a share of the money, I must admit that under the leadership of men like Mr. Tackaberry of Kapuskasing, Mr. Alex. Sterling, Mr. Tom Ripley and Mr. Law of Matheson, officials of the Northern Development Branch, who are active workers, we have no patronage under the present distribution of federal money through the provincial government. But I do not believe the head men of the Northern Ontario Development Department are always familiar with the situation. There are some minor officials who will go so far as to say that no Liberal will be given employment on road work. Once the situa-

Unemployment-Mr. Bradette
tion is known to the authorities, the present sitting members in the Ontario legislature, Mr. A. V. Waters and Mr. A. F. Kenning, no political nomination will interfere with a man working for the Northern Ontario Development department. I gladly make that statement.
My view is that there are three things which are holding back the prosperity of northern Ontario and which are also incidental to the prosperity of Canada as a whole. First of all is the question of agriculture, and I am going to reserve the right to speak on that matter when the agriculture estimates are presented to the house. There is a question I wish to ask of the Minister of Labour to-morrow or a few days hence in regard to the scheme which he mentioned this afternoon and has mentioned on several occasions, in connection with which the party received a great deal of publicity, having to do with the placing of thousands of people on the land in the last eighteen months with the help of the transportation systems. Last year I asked a question in the house and I received no reply. But again following the footsteps of the present Minister of Labour, I wish to speak of the wonderful rural districts in my constituency which are well suited for agricultural purposes. The districts of Cochrane are among the finest rural districts in Canada, showing an increase of 800 per cent in the last eighteen years, but I have yet to see a single person who has been placed on a farm there under this scheme mentioned by the Minister of Labour. I am going to ask the minister, how many people have been placed on the farms in North Timiskaming under the federal government scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to
look up the figures for the hon. member, but I do not have them before me at the moment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
It has also been stated that this scheme did not cost the federal administration a penny. Everybody knows that the transportation systems are not going to help finance the settlers further than bringing in their effects. I say as a settler myself, knowing the situation as it is in the rural sections of the country, that it is absolutely ridiculous-that is the proper word-to put anybody on the land unless he is going to receive assistance from the federal or provincial government. There should be a special grant. It is not sufficient to place those settlers on the farms; they must also be helped. The Minister of Labour knows his section of the country as I know mine, and he knows perfectly well that if you take

a man from Ottawa, Toronto or any other industrial centre and place him on a farm in northern Ontario, he cannot succeed unless he is helped by the federal or the provincial government. To-day we have not merely dozens but hundreds of families in our section of the country who are near starvation. I intend to take this matter up when the estimates are under consideration. Like the minister I have at heart the settlement of northern Ontario, but I repeat, it is not playing the game with our future farmers to place them on land in northern Ontario, old Quebec or the western provinces unless they get sufficient financial support from the provincial or federal authorities to enable them to carry on at least during the initial years of farming.
I wish to say a word about the pulpwood question. Naturally we have no quarrel with the east or the west. We settlers in northern Ontario have been very glad to see the western farmers getting from ten to twelve million dollars through the bonus on their wheat. In northern Ontario we are in an unhappy situation in that we cannot even give away the primary product that we have on our bush land. If the government find it possible to bonus the wheat grower they should also find it possible to bonus the settlers who have pulpwood for their first crop. In our section outside of a limited market, all pulpwood dealers are at present offering pulpwood at $3.50 a cord, and at that price, as every hon. member knows, it is absolutely impossible for them to butter their bread. One of the planks that was included in the platform of the Conservative party at the last general election was the prohibition of the free export of pulpwood. They declared for a policy that would prohibit the free export of pulpwood so as not to allow it to be shipped to keep American mills operating while Canadian mills are working part time. That statement was made during the last general election not only by my hon. friend from East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) but by Mr. Finlayson, the Minister of Mines and Forests for Ontario and by the federal Conservative party as a whole; and by reason of those declarations the American market which we had for our pulpwood was entirely disrupted. In my constituency there are three large newsprint mills with a daily capacity sufficient to supply the requirements of all the newspapers of Canada, and under those conditions it is absolutely necessary that we find an outside market for newsprint.
There is another angle to this situation. These mills must necessarily buy within a certain radius of their mills. The mill at

Unemployment-Mr. Bradette
Iroquois Falls, for instance, cannot buy pulp-wood east, west, north or south at a further distance than one hundred miles from the mill; consequently the farmers who are outside that area must find an outside market for their pulpwood. The only logical market we have for that pulpwood is the American market. During the last general election every American buyer in the Hearst district along the Canadian National, the Algoma Central, was withdrawn on account of the threatened restrictions on the export of pulpwood if the Conservative party came into power. I speak of my own knowledge. Our rural population are absolutely relying for their existence on pulpwood as the first crop while they are opening up the land, and unless they are able to dispose of that crop they cannot remain on the land. I hope that the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) will come out with a clear-cut statement and say that no restrictions will be placed on the export of pulpwood to the United States. Some people may say that there are no restrictions now. That may be so, but the threat of restrictions has disturbed the equilibrium of the pulpwood situation in northern Ontario. Persons competent to speak on this matter made that statement to me several times.
The other day, during the discussion of the potato situation in New Brunswick, we were told that the potato growers were given special freight rates so that they could market their potatoes in Ontario and Quebec. Unluckily for us in northern Ontario there are no preferential freight rates for any of the products that we produce. Last fall I was told by a pulpwood dealer that a contract for fifty thousand cords of pulpwood was turned down because on applying to the Canadian National railway board for a special rate it was denied the freight rates as applied in 1914. I maintain that it is the duty of this government to make the rulings of the railway board flexible enough so that in times of emergency like the present we may be granted special rates which would enable us to market our pulpwood in the American market.
I want to say a word about the trans-Canada highway, which is all important to northern Ontario. Every Conservative and Liberal candidate in the last election declared in favour of it. They were an absolute unit. The only difference of opinion between them was that some were not going far or fast enough. Some visualized the complete construction of the road within three years, others
within ten years. The people of northern Ontario remember, whether they heard it from the lips of the present Minister of Labour or the Conservative or Liberal candidates in northern Ontario, that they were all a unit for the building of the trans-Canada highway through that section of the country to provide a connecting link between the east and west, a road that would go through all Canadian territory.
Last year at Winnipeg or Regina the present Prime Minister made a statement that the trans-Canada highway would be routed over the Ferguson highway. The hon. member for East Algoma has also promised us a compromised highway, which I think has been pretty well accepted by the province of Ontario, so far as the route is concerned, but to my regret no work has been done over that section of the Ferguson highway except to straighten and widen some parts of it. South of Hearst in the Coppell section we were hoping that they would commence work on the road building towards Kenora, Fort William and Port Arthur, north of the great lakes. The government owes it to itself as well as to northern Ontario to carry out the promise which was distinctly made, and which the people clearly understood, to commence work on this trans-Canada highway. It ill behooves any member of the Conservative party to come into our section now and say that the Conservative party did not make any such promise. The promise was distinctly made. It is true that there are divergent opinions as to the route. The Minister of Labour himself was outspoken as to the route. It was a foregone conclusion that it was to be over the Ferguson highway. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) has also spoken of the trans-Canada highway going up to Fort William. Nevertheless the fact remains that the government should come out with a clear cut policy in this matter. Before the present High Commissioner for Canada in London left this country he made the statement, in the fall of 1930, that the routing of the trans-Canada highway rested entirely on the shoulders of the present government. So far no government, either provincial or federal, has dared to commit itself as to that routing. I may tell the present government that the people in northern Ontario are becoming impatient, but are hoping they will receive fair treatment. I repeat that during the last election campaign all candidates were in acoord so far as the building of the trans-

Unemployment-Mr. Bradette
Canada highway was concerned and its going through northern Ontario.
This afternoon the Minister of Labour quoted several letters dealing with the present situation. I also am going to quote certain articles from a Conservative newspaper. Fortunately in my district there are three good weekly newspapers, the Kapuskasing Tribune, of Kapuskasing, the Northland Post, of Cochrane, and the Porcupine Advance, of Timmins. Those three newspapers have the prosperity and advancement of northern Ontario at heart. The Minister of Railways and Canals tried to create the impression that the unemployment situation was not acute in northern Ontario. To refute that statement I am going to read some of the articles written in those newspapers. Turning to the Porcupine Advance of November 12, 1931, I find the following under the heading "Fair Play Needed":
Apparently the powers that be do not realize the seriousness of the unemployment situation in the north land. There are still hundreds of unemployed at Timmins, at Kirkland Lake, at Cochrane and at other places in the north, and up to the present moment nothing material has been done by the government of Ontario to relieve the situation. In the case of Timmins, one hundred men, out of a thousand or more, have been provided with employment in the past few weeks. What is to be done with the others? Press reports suggest that Hon. Mr. Finlayson indicates that the municipalities will be expected to care for their own married men. Such a suggestion is like Tim Buck's revolution it doesn't mean what it semes to imply. According to Tim Buck revolution isn't revolution but rather a state of mind. Hon. Mr. Finlayson's suggestion that each town should care for its own unemployed does not mean that at all, but rather it implies an inferiority complex or a pain in the neck. It should be remembered that Timmins, for instance, has already cared for all its own and a thousand over. There is not an industry or business or concern in Timmins that is not employing as many as a year or more ago. No men have been thrown out of work in Timmins during the past year or two, practically speaking. Instead there have been fully two thousand men come in here and fully half of these have been absorbed. That means in other words that Timmins has cared for all its own and a thousand besides and now the suggestion is made that the town care for a thousand others from the ends of the earth. Toronto, Hamilton, Ottawa, Winnipeg and scores of other cities have had industries close down or go on part time. Are these cities caring for their unemployed? Thousands of men have been taken from the south and a few from northern centres to work on the trans-Canada highway, but not a man has been moved from Timmins, or Cochrane, or Kirkland Lake to the trans-Canada work. Where is the sense or the justice or the fairness behind the attitude adopted? Who is responsible? There is a growing belief that much of the trouble rests with Hon. Mr. Finlayson. If this is a correct guess, there will inevitably develop a demand that Hon. Mr. 
Finlayson be replaced by a man with some sympathy for the north, or at least one willing to give this section of country something like a fair deal. The town of Timmins is very willing to do its share and more. It has already contributed more than its fair share to unemployment relief. The government has approved a .$60,000 program of necessary work planned by Timmins but even though this is actually designed to relieve unemployment of outsiders who have drifted to Timmins and are now out of work themselves or have displaced Timmins men in employment, the government apparently is seeking to evade its responsibility for these outsiders and to lay the whole burden on the town. Though approving the whole $60,000 worth of work for relief, the government is ready so far to contribute a share of only $20,000 of the amount. The attention of the government is directed to the fact that the people of Timmins are not able to shoulder the burden thrust upon them. There are literally hundreds of people here who find it a hardship to meet tax bills as they are now. Some are unable to pay their taxes at all. The general conditions and special circumstances are felt by many in serious way. Is it fair or right to overburden the taxpayers of Timmins to support the unemployed hundreds who are clearly and surely the responsibility of the province, not the town?
I wish to say a few words concerning statistics which have been recited by the Minister of Labour. He stated this afternoon that as a result of unemployment relief measures, some 334,000 people have been given work. I do not doubt his figure, but all sorts of stunts can be done with them and I should like more elaborate statements. I should like to hear the number of hours worked, the occupations, and so on. I have in mind hundreds of people in my own riding who have only ten or twenty days' work during the year, and who receive S2.40 per day for their work. Married men are allowed to work only three days a week, making only about 8360 in a year, if they could find employment for the whole year. Worse than that, however, a single man is allowed to work only two days per week, and in that new section of the country we have a great number of unmarried men who have come among us to hew out a living. I can see no reason why there should be such a restriction against single men.
When the Minister of Labour mentioned that at the large salary of S7.20 per week there is really no starvation I was tempted to think that those people must be near starvation. In my own riding I know that there are families who have not the clothing to go to church or to mix with their friends, and because of that are even deprived of fresh air. I know of people eating potatoes three times a day, and who have been doing so for the last three months. These are facts; and if possible I should like some government

Unemployment-Mr. Bradette
official to go to northern Ontario, particularly to North Timiskanaing, and see for himself the conditions existing up there in some of the rural sections.
' I believe the Minister of Labour is sincere in his statement. I well remember that last summer during the provincial election campaign in the province of Quebec he told the settlers in that province that if they wanted roads they ought to come to Ontario. I am glad to learn that in his opinion the settlers in South Timiskaming have all the roads they require. I want to say to him that in my own riding there are settlers who have been on their places for the last fifteen or twenty years and who still have to pack the provisions for their families on account of lack of roads. If they have all the roads they require in South Timiskaming I hope the minister, out of his kindness of heart, will use all influence with the federal and provincial authorities to see that the settlers get work on the roads to which they were entitled a number of years ago. I took the statement he made in the province of Quebec at par value; I wanted to believe it represented the actual fact; I hope that every settler in those northern constituencies will have all the roads they require in the very near future. May I say, however, that in this year of grace 1932 in North Timiskaming there are hundreds of settlers who have not the road facilities to which they are entitled.
At this point may I refer to some comments made in the Porcupine Advance of December 31, 1932:
Anyone who gives any particular thought to the matter will regret to note the sad failure made by the province of Ontario in dealing with the unemployment problem. The Dominion government attacked the problem in a big way and left the path open for the province to deal effectively and successfully with the difficulty. Instead of extended work on a broad scale, the province seems to have been overwhelmed by the situation and the effort to right matters has been spasmodic and panicky. Most of the battle has been left to the municipalities and even the towns and cities have not received the support deserved. In the case of Timmins, for instance, while all the program planned by the town was approved by the commission in charge, only part of it came in for assistance from the government, though the whole program was designed for the relief of people who are clearly a provincial or dominion responsibility and not a local one. The camp is employing over a thousand men more than two years ago, and yet had a thousand men out of work, this meaning that all the unemployment here was caused by men drifting in from other centres. In the apportionment of men for work on the trans-Canada highway there has been no quota from Timmins. Towns and cities where the unemployment has originated have been helped unduly, at the expense of other centres that were ready to
care for a proportion of the unemployed of other places. Only a hundred men have been taken from Timmins for work at the special camps of the northern development department. The first hundred men have been returned and another hundred taken in their place, the matter thus resolving itself into a part time employment at a wage rate too low for decent living even under steady employment. With a number of public works very necessary for the advantage of the country-such as the road connecting up the mining camps of Sudbury, Shining-tree, Elk Lake, Matachewan, and Porcupine

it would be possible to provide work for all, to the general advantage. It may be argued that there is not money for these works. In case of such an argument there will be a general demand to know where the money has all gone, and also if there is no money for public works under which men may preserve their independence and the country receive some benefit, there is yet money for direct relief. Indeed a premium is placed on direct relief by municipalities, the government giving a larger grant for such relief than for the better form of relief-the only sensible form of relief-work for the unemployed. The people of Canada do not want relief of the charity type. They simply want some of their own money, and for this they are willing to work for the common benefit.
Hundreds of men out of work in Timmins, though the town has done more than its share for the relief of unemployment by the providing of work! Hundreds out of work in other towns of the north, and elsewhere throughout Ontario! All this after the government has had months to prepare and arrange affairs!
The government should turn over a new leaf for the new year. There should be earnestness and efficiency shown in the work of the relief of the unemployed. Had it not been for incidental matters that provided employment; had it not been for the work undertaken by municipalities; and had it not been for the remarkably mild weather this year, the province would have more serious hardship for a large number of men than the amount that has been encountered. and that amount has been altogether too much.
In the new year the government should take up the unemployment question in a different attitude altogether. No thought should be given to the preservation of profits for any who have already made big money from the resources of the province. There should be no care for the feelings of the high finance group. There should be system and efficiency established, with the sole idea in mind of relieving unemployment by means of providing necessary and valuable work that will benefit the country and people.
The Dominion government has a blank cheque for the relief of unemployment. This blank cheque has been passed on, as it were, to the provinces. Should there be more money spent than the people think has been possible in Ontario from the comparatively small amount of relief provided, and if the end of Ontario's share is in sight, then the province can safely come to the people for more funds. It is certain that the people in general are absolutely opposed to the idea of anyone starving to death, or even suffering hardship. There is a very general feeling that unemployment must be relieved. There are only two ways to relieve it, the one being by direct relief and the other by providing work. The system of direct relief is

Unemployment-Mr. Bradette
against all the ideas of tlie people of Canada. To the average Canadian the only sensible plan seems to be to provide work. In this the government will receive the fullest support. The government should start the new year right by getting some system into its relief work program and seeing that the ordinary run of men get a fair deal.
Having regard to the severity of the unemployment situation in northern Ontario I desire to give the viewpoint of the rural population. The Minister of Labour said in reference to the letters that he had received from the various organized municipalities that the local authorities were prepared to look after the relief work. But we must not lose sight of the fact that most of the rural districts of northern Ontario are not organized. Consequently all the responsibility for attending to relief work in these sections falls on the provincial government. There are sections in my own riding that have been opened up for settlement for the last twenty years, but they are still unorganized, and up to date the people there have not received anything by way of unemployment relief. In this connection I desire to read to the house a letter I received this morning from the president of the local settlers' association of Mattice. He writes under date of February 20, 1932:
Yours of the 1st inst., duly came to hand, and we greatly appreciate your loyal support to relieve distress in this section, although this is not altogether under the direct control of the authorities at Ottawa. However being aware that you have done all in your power, and in turn we have not pointed out to you the general injustice felt, as we had hopes that a change was to take place locally, in accord with promise made by the engineer in writing; however no change took place and nothing is being done yet to relieve conditions locally. With this in mind we feel that we should draw your attention to the following facts:
1.	Relief was demanded for reason already stated, and nothing has been done although promises were made.
2.	The northern department of development undertook to complete the gravelling from Mattice, starting at mileage 103 to Opesatika by trucks.
3.	Married men were given employment at the gravel pit three days during week and single men two days during week, and the number of men is very small and not providing for a fair revenue to those without revenue.
4.	Regular employment on this job, was given to mostly all men from outside (men from Hearst and Cochrane), and Mattice could have provided for some of this employment; why was it not done?
("A" They brought in a man from outside to cut wood for stoves, a single man. Men couMhave been found at Mattice for this job.
"B" They brought in a man from outside to keep fire going in the camps during the night. Men could have been found in Mattice for this job.

"C" They brought in a man from Cochrane to check gravel at the other end, when there is a man already doing this, in this case we feel it is duplicate work for nothing.
"D" They brought in men from outside to put up a small garage with lumber and a little tarred paper. Men in Mattice could have done this work.
"E" All trucks are employed six days during the week. Though this comes under the necessary relief to relieve local distress, all these men are from outside.
"F" They have a man to operate a tractor for snow ploughing who is more or less idle but on regular weekly pay. This same man has a truck of his own running on the roads hauling gravel, but employing another man in its place, this man is a single man and the son of local road inspector at Hearst.)
5.	We understand that relief money voted by the federal authorities was to be spent in the interest of localities affected and in need of work for his own people and the provincial authority was to administer these funds. At Mattice, Fryatt. MacBay, and Reesar, nothing is done to give work to settlers in need.
6.	If it was necessary to gravel the road for automobiles from outside, for which settlers have no use, why employ trucks altogether. This work could have been done on a fair basis by permitting the trucks to gravel the long distance travelling east and permitting the teams from settlers to get on and gravel the short distance travelling west, as understood and promised by the provincial authorities, this on about December 1st. At that time they were aware of our need and promised the work: since then nothing has been done to give to the settlers a little revenue. We are in need of revenue by the means of work, if they knew of our need. How long will it take to overcome the distress? Promises do not give a man on a lot something to eat for his family and permit him to meet his obligations.
We have already a case of a settler on a well settled farm, owing to the fact he could not get work for his horses, and not being able to afford to feed his two horses all winter doing nothing, he decided to kill the poorest one. Will this last much longer?
I feel it is not necessary to enter into very many details of this sort, for you know our general conditions. It would require very little to help us to see the year over, and this we ask and must obtain in the form of work.
In a few days now many many teams will be done hauling the little pulpwood there was to haul, and what are we going to do?
We understand that some men made the statement that the settlers in this section were well off and did not need relief work. Why this statement? I presume it is in the form of punishment which is not needed, for we have enough of the actual distress without allowing such statements to be made and taken as granted that we are not in need of work. These statements is merely made by the man or men as their personal views, and are not correct.
My dear Mr. Bradette, is it not possible apparently to obtain satisfaction within our needs? By good will we all urge you to bring up our cause to the proper authorities again, and if necessary take the matter up in House of Commons of Canada. We are Canadians and we want to be Canadians. Through you, our representative, we demand action.

Unemployment-Mr. Fournier
Previous to the last election during the debates in this house certain ho'n. members put the onus on the government of relieving unemployment on the ground that it had become so serious that it was a national matter. During the last election the Conservative party stated that unemployment was purely and simply a federal matter, and if they were returned to power it would be so dealt with at once without any red tape. I know that the Hon. Mr. Finlayson, Minister of Lands and Forests in the provincial cabinet, has been down to Ottawa on different occasions, and the officials of the northern development branch have told the settlers in my section of the country, and rightly so, that if they did not get the relief work they were entitled to it was because the federal government had not made the necessary grant to the provincial authorities. The Canadian people are alive to the situation and are giving the fullest latitude to the government to apply adequate remedies. On January 31, the Mail and Empire contained the following despatch from Ottawa:
Ontario Asks Funds For Highway Work
Request for Further Appropriation Presented to Federal Cabinet Finlayson in Ottawa
Ottawa, Jan. 31.-The Dominion Cabinet has under consideration the request of the Ontario government for further appropriations to make it possible to continue work on the trans-Canada highway. Hon. William Finlayson, Ontario Minister of Lands and Forests, was in Ottawa on Saturday, when he laid before some of the ministers the need for additional appropriations.
Hon. William Finlayson, who was in Ottawa Saturday conferring with the Dominion government regarding further finances for the trans-Canada and other Northern Ontario road relief projects, stated last night that he expected a definite reply from Premier Bennett to-day on the situation.
Mr. Finlayson declined to say what appropriation is required to carry the road work on until April as originally scheduled, or what the province had asked the federal authorities to contribute further in this regard.
Premier George S. Henry to-night stated work on the trans-Canada highway in Ontario had progressed with unexpected speed owing to mild weather prevailing throughout the areas in which construction camps are situated.
The result, he said, had been that more money was already spent than officials had anticipated. The original estimates provided funds to carry work on until April 1. The province and the dominion provided the money on a fifty-fifty basis. Mr. Henry said he could not immediately determine the amount of money remaining from the original appropriation, nor the length of time it would be possible to carry on the work without calling for more funds. Eventually, he said, more money would have to be appropriated.
I know the Prime Minister is anxious to relieve unemployment, and therefore I make this statement to him that on the first of April all the money distributed for unemployment relief in the province of Ontario will have been spent, but there will still be unemployment. This is the worst time of the year for our settlers in northern Ontario, for if they are not able to earn sufficient money to buy seed grain and keep their families in food and clothing they will have to abandon their holdings and come down to the already overcrowded urban centres. I make an earnest appeal to the government-and if the Minister of Labour were in his seat I know he would cooperate with me, because he knows the situation as well as I do-I make an earnest appeal to the government that more money be appropriated for the unemployed in the rural and industrial sections of northern Ontario, that more road work be undertaken so that it may be carried on well into June and July. I am making this appeal in the hope that the government, being now familiar with the seriousness of conditions in northern Ontario, will devise a plan to relieve the pressing necessities of the population there, otherwise they will find it impossible to remain on their holdings or keep their property. In the name of my constituents, in the name of the fine type of people of whom the Minister of Labour spoke this afternoon, I make this fervent appeal to the government to take such measures as will enable them to carry on their work of opening up for Canada and for the world that wonderful section of the dominion that we call northern Ontario.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
I
shall be very brief in my remarks, Mr. Speaker, but I was induced to speak on this motion after listening to the remarks of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), who quoted figures to show to what extent the government had helped to relieve unemployment throughout the country. He stated that in 1930 no one knew exactly how long this depression would last or what its intensity would be, and he also said that if it had been a normal depression the measures adopted by the government certainly would have had a good effect and would have relieved unemployment to a greater extent.
The minister stated that 870,570,080 was spent in 1930 throughout the country on relief work, and that the share of this government was about $14,000,000. He also stated that this provided work for 332,000 individuals. He stopped his figures at that point, but I think he should have gone further and stated how many days these 332,000 people had

4S2

Unemployment-Mr. Fournier
worked. It would have been found that they had worked only a little over seven million days. Going further, we find that during 1930 these people worked an average of 23 days during the entire year; that was the extent of the relief given the unemployed by relief work. If we were to calculate the amount spent as compared with the number of individuals receiving relief, we would find that each working day given these people cost the municipal, provincial and federal governments about $10, and in 1931 the figures were not much improved. Up to January 1 of this year $60,000,000 was spent on relief work, giving work to 285,000 people, who averaged 11 days work per person. The share of the federal government in that relief work amounted to about $28,000,000.
It must be remembered that in addition to relief work the government gave money for direct relief. In 1930 this amounted to about $2,000,000, according to the Financial Post of January 20. This amount helped some 430,770 heads of families and single people, so that the $2,000,000 spent on direct relief, together with the $5,000,000 provided by provincial and municipal governments for that purpose, helped more people than were helped by the relief work which has been carried on at much greater cost.
After the minister said that no one knew how long the depression would last or what intensity it would reach I was tempted to ask what measures the government would have taken had they known this depression was world-wide; I was anxious to learn what other means they could have employed to relieve conditions. The minister was silent on that matter; he only stated that people throughout the country were kept from starvation through the actions of this government. I must remind the house that when this depression started in 1929 the revenues of the country were going down, so the money spent for relief had to be borrowed. This $70,000,000 was secured in that way and added to the funded debts of the municipal, provincial and federal governments, so there must be added to our obligations a further amount of about three millions, being amount of interest on that borrowed money.
The largest part of this money was spent on public works, such as buildings, highways and bridges. We did not actually need a great many of these buildings and highways, or at least they could have waited for normal times when the cost would have been lower. Surely some other scheme to aid unemployment could have been devised. I still believe the government should have helped 
by direct grants to the provincial governments and the municipalities, because in that way more people would have been assisted.
As to local conditions in the city of Hull, I may say that we have about two thousand people unemployed or employed on part time. The different industries in Hull are working on part time, and since we have also a certain number of civil servants, we will suffer still more if the proposed bill concerning civil servants is passed. Since September 1 last we have spent nearly $75,000 on direct relief, which amount has been contributed by the municipal, provincial and federal governments, but every day we have unemployed persons stopping us on the streets or calling at our houses for food. They are so destitute that they have not the pride that enables people to bear up under this depression. Hull is not a very rich city; it is composed in the main of labourers, and when our few industries close theiir doors necessarily these people must rely on help coming from the different governments. Of the two thousand people I am told that about four hundred received one week's work out of four in the city.
As to the city of Ottawa, where unemployment should not be known, I riiould like to quote from the Citizen of a few days ago. The article is headed "Work for Ottawa Women", and states:
Yesterday in Ottawa some devoted members of the Local Council of Women opened a workroom where destitute women can be given an opportunity to earn a few dollars weekly. The plan is to give out sewing and mending work. On the first day more than 130 women applied. Some were receiving temporary relief through the welfare bureau, but they are women who want work rather than a charitable ration of food.
